chapters.summary: Council staff calls the hearing to order. Chair Sandra Ung welcomes attendees, recognizes committee members Encarnación, Carr, and Abreu, and acknowledges committee counsel and staff who prepared the hearing.
chapters.title: Chair Ung opens hearing and introduces committee members and staff

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to today's New York City Council hearing on the Committee on Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards, and Ectus.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: At this time, no one may approach the dais.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please silence all electronic devices.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Chair, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Good morning and welcome to this meeting of the Committee on Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards, and Ethics.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Sandra Ung, Chair of the Committee.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Before we begin, I would like to recognize the other members of the committee who are present.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Councilmember Elsie Encarnación, and Minority Leader David Carr, and Majority Leader Shaun-Abreu.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I would also like to acknowledge the acting counsel to the committee, Maka Ajabi, and committee staff that worked on today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The director and deputy director of the council's public integrity unit, Per Moore and Lee Shabassel, associate general counsel, Amanda Del Grasso, as well as other attorneys and compliance professionals in the office of general counsel who helped to prepare this hearing.

chapters.summary: Ung announces the committee will consider three nominations: Lisa Garcia for the NYC Land Bank Board, Dr. Dave Chokshi for the Board of Health, and John Mangin as Chair of the Board of Standards and Appeals, in that order.
chapters.title: Chair Ung outlines three mayoral nominations before the committee

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Today, the committee will consider the mayor's nomination of DEP Commissioner Lisa Garcia to be a member of the New York City Land Bank's Board of Directors.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Dr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Dave Chukshi to be a member of the Board of Health, and John Mangin to be both a member and the chair of the Board of Standards and Appeals.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We'll begin the nomination of Commissioner Garcia, then we'll hear from Dr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Chukshi, and then conclude.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Manjin.

chapters.summary: Ung explains the Land Bank's seven-member board, real estate experience requirements, mission to preserve homeownership and prevent displacement, and the working group's task to seek state approval for establishment. Board members serve four-year terms without pay.
chapters.title: Chair Ung provides background on NYC Land Bank under Local Law 56 of 2026

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: By the letter dated August 7, 2026, and pursuant to Local Law 56 of 2026, Mayor Mandani requested the Council's advice and consent regarding his nomination of DEP Commissioner Lisa Garcia to be a member of New York City Land Bank's Board of Directors.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Local Law 56 of 2026 provides that upon the approval of New York State Urban Development Corporation, the City of New York will establish a land bank.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: There will be seven members of the Board of Directors of the land bank, unless adjusted in accordance with its bylaws.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: A member of the Board of Directors must have appropriate experience with real estate and be a resident of New York City throughout their service on the board.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The land bank will seek to preserve the ownership and equity interests of homeowners, prevent the displacement of residents from their dwellings, and promote the productive use of tax-for-clothes, vacant, and abandoned properties to meet the needs of the surrounding communities and city.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: In conjunction with the enforcement of tax liens, individuals initially appointed to the Board of Directors shall serve as a working group to prepare a necessary application for New York State Urban Development Corporation's approval of the establishment of a land bank.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Members of the Board of Directors for a land bank serve a four-year term without pay.

chapters.summary: Ung details Garcia's appointment as DEP Commissioner in February 2026, her prior role as EPA Region 2 Regional Administrator, her work at Grist Magazine and Earthjustice, and her Juris Doctorate from Brooklyn Law School.
chapters.title: Chair Ung introduces Commissioner Lisa Garcia's professional background

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We are joined today by Lisa Garcia, Commissioner of the New York City Department of Environmental Protections.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Commissioner Garcia was appointed to lead the agency in February 2026.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: In this position, she helped protect the city's infrastructure and environment, ensured that the delivery of the high-quality service such as drinking water, such as drinking water,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: and storage treatment, and make sure the city is a global leader in the fight against the climate crisis.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Prior to DEP, Commissioner Garcia served the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Environmental Protection Agency's regional administrator for Region 2, overseeing the Biden administration's environmental agenda in New York, New Jersey, Puerto Rico, and the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Virgin Islands and the eight Indian nations.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: She ran the Climate Solutions Lab at Grist Magazine, where she worked to elevate climate justice leaders and have served as a vice president for litigation at the Earth Justice, as well as associate administrator at the EPA.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Commissioner Garcia holds a Juris Doctorate degree from Brooklyn Law School.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I now recognize the committee counsel to administer affirmation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your statements before this committee and response to all questions posed by the council members?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Well, please have a seat.

chapters.summary: Garcia describes her career focus on environmental justice and community outreach, emphasizing her experience bringing stakeholders together. She highlights how community engagement will be paramount for the Land Bank's success.
chapters.title: Lisa Garcia opening statement: environmental justice experience and community engagement

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Good morning, Commissioner Garcia.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I recognize you now make an opening statement.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Ong and members of the Committee on Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards, and Ethics.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I'm Lisa Garcia, Commissioner for the Department of Environmental Protection.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I'm here today because I have the honor of being considered for the appointment to the New York City Land Bank Board of Directors.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Before coming to DEP, I served as Regional Administrator for the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: EPA, the Environmental Protection Agency, Region 2, covering New York, New Jersey, Puerto Rico, the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Virgin Islands, and eight Indian nations, mainly upstate New York.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I've also worked in environmental journalism, environmental law, and advocacy.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Throughout my career, my focus has been on environmental justice, climate protection, and community outreach.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I have experience bringing stakeholders together in many different forums and venues to gather input and feedback on a variety of issues.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: of challenging issues, all with the goal of trying to collectively find solutions.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Should I be appointed to the Land Bank Board of Directors, I would draw from my experience in government, academia, and non-for-profit organizations representing community groups.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: My robust

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: background, I think, in environmental justice and community engagement would especially inform my work on the land bank.

chapters.summary: Garcia outlines the Land Bank's dual role of collecting owed revenue and transferring delinquent properties to better public uses. She connects DEP's lien sale work to the land bank's mission and expresses excitement about helping establish the new entity.
chapters.title: Lisa Garcia opening statement: land bank vision and DEP's role in collections

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I wanted to highlight my experience in community engagement because community and stakeholder engagement will be paramount for the land bank's success.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Should I be part of the land bank board of directors, I would prioritize making sure that there was a robust process for engagement so that all parties and interests could be heard.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I propose meeting with the council members, the committee members, reaching out directly to some of the most vocal and interested stakeholders, and hosting roundtables with different partners to get a well-rounded set of recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: The stakeholders must include representatives from different areas of expertise and represent different constituencies.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: While housing is one area of input to the board,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: that we should seek.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: For example, there are many other stakeholders that need to be involved.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I expect that the Land Bank Board of Directors would work closely as a group and with the Council to identify a variety of stakeholders who would bring an array of interests and backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: The legislation that created the Land Bank

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: requires the city to transition away from the trust-based lien sale to this land bank model by 2029.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: The land bank's primary mission is to provide a process that is equitable, accountable, and transparent in collecting outstanding property taxes and water and sewer bills.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I understand that the vision for the land bank is to have dual roles, to collect owed revenue and debt,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: and also to transfer delinquent properties into uses that better serve the public interest, such as affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I look forward to helping set up this new entity as soon as possible, if confirmed.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Currently, DEP uses the lien sale as a tool to collect unpaid water and sewer bills on certain properties and bring customers into good standing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Bringing customers into good standing has always been our priority.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: DEP's goal is to balance customer needs and fairness while collecting unpaid debt.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Which is in line with the goals of the land bank.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: This work is a natural extension of my role as DEP Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I'm excited by the prospect of working with the Council, land bank board members, and members of the public to ensure that the land bank is efficient and effective

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: while reflecting the sensitivities around home ownership and property sales.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I'm excited for the opportunity to be

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: be part of this important endeavor.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I thank this committee for considering my nomination, and I'm happy to answer any questions that you have.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We are also joined by council members, Hanif and Krishnan.

chapters.summary: Ung asks about Garcia's understanding of the land bank's vision. Garcia describes transitioning from the trust-based lien sale to a more equitable, accountable, and transparent model with flexibility for property reuse.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Garcia on land bank vision and purpose

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm going to start with a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm going to pass it off to my other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So first, what is your understanding and the purpose of the vision for the New York City Land Bank?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: My understanding is one, to transition away from the current trust-based lien sale

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: to this land bank model, really with an eye towards being more equitable, accountable, and transparent than...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: In collecting outstanding properties and outstanding water and sewer bills.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Again, with this eye towards collection, but also making sure that the transfer of delinquent properties could go into better uses to serve the public.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And so there's a lot more flexibility and opportunities with a land bank.

chapters.summary: Ung asks about powers conferred on land banks by New York State. Garcia discusses the flexibility land banks provide for holding and reusing properties while taking community concerns into account.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Garcia on land bank powers and policy goals

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: New York State confers a number of powers upon the land banks.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: What is your understanding of what the powers a land bank generally are, and can you describe how you think they'll be used further, the policy goals of a land bank?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: My understanding is that once you get the approval from the state, again, that there's a lot more

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: flexibility with the land banks, a lot more options, and the options for this process to be

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: designed, again, with holding properties in the bank, but also with a plan to possibly reuse properties in different ways and taking into account community concerns.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ung asks how the land bank can improve on past tools for revenue collection and housing preservation. Garcia emphasizes community outreach and engagement as key to designing a better process.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Garcia on improving collection tools while preserving housing

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And how do you think the land bank can improve upon the city's past and current use of available tools to collect revenues while preserving existing housing and creating new housing?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think that one thing, as I mentioned, the land bank does have those opportunities and flexibility.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I wouldn't want to prejudge what the final outcome would be.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: But again, if you think of the remit from this legislation to the land bank directors, it would really be to think of what are the concerns of the community?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: How do we respond to the concerns with the past processes and create a new processes that meets the moment of, again, the equity, accountability, transparency?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So in designing it, community.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: outreach and engagement will be paramount to get us to that place.

chapters.summary: Garcia identifies efficiency and effectiveness in implementing new procedures as the biggest challenge, noting NYC's land bank is unique in combining collections with community-focused property reuse, unlike other cities' models.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Garcia on greatest challenge facing the land bank

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And what do you think would be the greatest challenge that the New York City Land Bank would face after it's established?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I think one of the biggest challenges with any new process put in place is making sure that it is effective and efficient.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So that's one thing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And I don't think it's...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: It's solely about this land bank.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: It's just putting in new procedures and processes.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And I think the other thing, having studied and talked to other cities that have used community land banks, this is really different because it's about there's a collections aspect and making sure that the city collects its

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: unpaid debt, but also looking towards that, how do you return the lands or think of properties in the lens of the community.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So New York City is really tasked with creating something a little bit different than what other land banks have been used for in the country that I've seen, that I've observed.

chapters.summary: Ung asks about Garcia's experience relevant to the board's real estate and planning requirements. Garcia cites DEP's work with the Department of Finance on lien sales and her experience running public engagement processes.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Garcia on relevant experience for land bank board

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: New York City Local Law 56 of 2026 requires that the members of the Board of Directors of the New York City Land Bank have appropriate experience in real estate, finance, property management, community planning and development, or other relevant fields.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Can you share information as to your past experience that you believe is pertinent to serving as a Board of Directors of the New York City Land Bank?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Yeah, so in my current role, I think there's a natural extension.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Because DEP has always worked with the Department of Finance on lien sales, DEP, as I mentioned, it collects unpaid water and sewer charges that may result in being transferred to the land bank or to the lien sale.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Also, my past experience having hosted public information meetings, running community engagement,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: running forums where we're gathering information to be able to create a new policy or a new law, I think that my past experience in that kind of

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: legal field and policy field and implementing governmental change is a real asset as a board member.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ung questions whether Garcia can balance DEP commissioner duties with the working group's demands. Garcia confirms she can, noting other commissioners are also appointed and praising her 6,000-person DEP team.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Garcia on time commitment for working group

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And pursuant to local law 56 of 2026, individuals initially appointed to serve on the board of directors of the land bank shall serve as a working group

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: to prepare the necessary application for approval from the state in relation to establishment of the land bank.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The task of preparing application could place significant demands on your time and attention and must be completed in a specific time frame.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: While serving as the commissioner of DEP, do you believe you'll be able to commit to the appropriate time and attention necessary to fulfill the duties of the working group?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Yes, I do think that I'll be able to fulfill the mission and working with the other members of the board.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I think that we'll all, as you know, there's other commissioners appointed.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I think that this is a really important task that we'll dedicate time to and make sure we come up with the correct design.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: and make the recommendations.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And on the other hand, I have to say I have a great team over at the Department of Environmental Protection, almost 6,000 people.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So it's a really good balance of being able to depend on those experts and professionals when I am in a meeting or like here at a hearing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ung asks which stakeholders the working group should solicit input from. Garcia identifies affordable housing advocates, community economic development nonprofits, and revitalization groups as starting points.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Garcia on stakeholder input requirements

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And pursuant to Local Law 56 of 2026, members of the working group must seek input for relevant stakeholders, including not-for-profit corporations

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: that operate in the City of New York to foster neighborhood stabilization and revitalization through protection, preservation, and development of properties that contain affordable housing, commercial uses, and community uses.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Can you identify some of the stakeholders from which you believe from the working group should solicit input?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Yes, obviously we think, I mean this is a really important piece of it that we create the new process with the sensitivities of understanding home ownership and how communities don't want to be displaced, certainly homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And so with that in mind, working with the council that created the law, we were talking about the purpose of local law, and also working with affordable housing advocates, community

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: economic development, economic revitalization nonprofit groups.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Those are the ones that I'm thinking that we would start out with.

chapters.summary: Garcia shares her experience with contentious environmental justice hearings, emphasizing her priority of listening to all affected stakeholders and bringing feedback back to the board.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Garcia on personal community engagement experience

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And can you speak a bit about your personal experience engaging with the kinds of stakeholders?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: from who you think working groups should solicit input from?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Yeah, I have a lot of experience, as I mentioned, in environmental justice.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And if you haven't been to a hearing on citing a power plant in a community of color, you must know that some of those get extremely contentious.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: But the goal is to remain and to listen to community members.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And so that is a real priority of mine, is to make sure that we're listening to all the affected stakeholders.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And we bring those recommendations, that feedback, back to the board, back to the land bank board, so that we really take into account some of the challenges that have happened in the past and also, of course, the best practices and lessons learned.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We also have Deputy Speaker Nantasha Williams on remote.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And right now I'm going to pass the question off to Council Member Krishnan.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks how the land bank can creatively preserve affordable housing through CLTs and HDFCs. Garcia discusses the opportunity to reuse delinquent properties for community purposes, citing examples from Baton Rouge and other cities.
chapters.title: CM Krishnan Q&A: Garcia on affordable housing preservation and community land trusts

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Commissioner, I know we're here in a different capacity, but it's good to see you again, and I appreciate all your work and your leadership of DEP.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I know we partnered together on many things in my community where flooding from Queens Boulevard to

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: 25th Avenue has been a big issue in our community, and I appreciate your partnership in trying to find sustainable long-term ways to address it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I just had a question for you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You know, with the land bank in particular, I also think there are opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: generally, to think creatively about how we preserve affordable housing in our city.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Community land trusts provide one example.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You know, HDFCs, which have fallen by the wayside, provide another example.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I've represented them, and I know how critical they are.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: These are all good tools to preserve affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I'm just wondering how you think about that.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: What is the role of the land bank in coming up with some creative solutions to preserve affordable housing?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Some of them, which frankly have existed before, but our city has moved away from them over the years, and it would be good to rethink how we can bring them back.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Or new ones like CLTs, which I think are really important tools as well.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How does a land bank oversee those issues or think about those issues, and how would you in this position think about them?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you so much for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And yes, thank you for the partnership.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So that's a really important question, and I think aspect of the land bank, having studied some other community land banks and land banks across the country,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: it really does set the stage for New York City to think of how we look at abandoned properties, what the reuse of the property is, with a lens towards...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Maybe improving or meeting or matching what the community's desires are.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And so I think right now, as I understand the process of the lien sale, it's very much about the sale.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And then, you know,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: you know, the private trust takes it over and usually just sells it.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: But here there's an opportunity to say, yes, we need to focus on the enforcement and collections.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: That's one goal.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: But the other is, then what?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Can we reuse that property?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And so that, I think I look forward to working with the board members to really think of those options, that flexibility.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And also, like I said before, some of the best practices from like Baton Rouge that is doing it, thinking of a main street and bringing back open space to a community or in the Palisades.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Fire in California they're thinking of standing up on with that idea of what would we do with this property into the future.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Yeah, so I think you hit the mark that there is those opportunities and I look forward to working with the council and all of you and everyone else on what those opportunities could be.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Abreu raises concerns about the lien sale list disproportionately targeting Black and brown homeowners and asks about foreclosure appropriateness and ensuring funds flow back to impacted communities. Garcia commits to addressing these issues as a core value.
chapters.title: CM Abreu Q&A: Garcia on lien sale list transparency and equity impacts

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And now I'd like to pass it to Majority Leader Brujo.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner, for coming to testify and answering Councilmember questions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Properties in the lien sale process in New York City are disproportionately located in a handful of neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Those that are generally occupied by black and brown homeowners, many of whom are facing gentrification pressures and predatory actors.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The current lien sale process requires a publication of all properties potentially eligible to be sold in the lien sale process.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This includes the owner's

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: only publicly accessible list that identifies properties with past due water bills, thereby making these properties an easy target for predatory actors.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Considering the immense concerns raised around publishing these kinds of lists when the city published the PETA terror list this year, do you think publishing the lien sale list is appropriate?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Especially considering that the lien sale list goes further than the PETA tear list in publicizing previously non-public information.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: I have heard the concerns about that, and that is certainly one thing that I look forward to talking to the other land bank members about.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Again, how do we improve this process?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And maybe that could be one of the questions that we consider.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: At what point do you think it is appropriate for the city, via the land bank, or directly to foreclose on a homeowner for non-payment of taxes or water bills?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Again, I think we'll be working together to figure out what the procedures are and what the protocol would be into the future.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And so it's difficult to kind of prejudge what that outcome would be.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: One of the concerns relating to the lien sale enforcement process in New York City and the associated disproportionate community impact is that it strips assets and wealth from communities, which then see no tangible improvements in return.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What can DEP do to ensure that these funds generated from this enforcement process are actually flowing?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: into the communities negatively impacted by enforcement.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So again, I usually, my experience is in working on equity, racial equity, environmental justice, and so I just lead with that kind of,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: those kinds of questions as a core value, and how do we ensure that there aren't unintended consequences with any new processes, policy, legal action that we take,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: because usually, unfortunately, the history in the United States shows that it does disproportionately impact communities of color and many times low-income communities.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And so that'll be definitely front and center of how I show up, how I participate,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: and make sure that, you know, as I said before, this seems like a great opportunity to think of this process, to be more equitable, accountable, and transparent.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And so I appreciate the question and the opportunity to join in that effort.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'd also like to acknowledge Councilman Brewer who has joined us today, but seeing no other members, I'm sorry, apologies, Councilman Brewer has a question.

chapters.summary: Brewer, who authored the land bank bill, asks what kinds of projects might fall under the land bank and how many properties might be eligible. Garcia says it's hard to predict but notes DEP's expanded affordability programs and door-knocking efforts to keep homeowners in good standing.
chapters.title: CM Brewer Q&A: Garcia on land bank project types and eligibility

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I've been listening on my cell phone, so congratulations.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: It's my bill, so I have a lot of positive feelings about it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: My question would be within the lean possibilities of DEP, even past or maybe even what you might think happening in the future,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: What kinds of projects do you think might fall under a land bank?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Ages and what do you think perhaps could happen?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is it a building?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is it an institution?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have any sense of where those lean sales, which could have been lean sales, hopefully will be land bank and nonprofit.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Could be taking place.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, within the portfolio, obviously you have lean sales possibility in your portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'm just wondering what the world might look like.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So I think that as we've been talking about, there is this ability in creating the land bank to really think of where those flexibilities and where those opportunities lie.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: And I think it's really incumbent as we're designing this, again, not only the community engagement and listening to what some of the stakeholders'concerns were, what the council's purpose of the law was, but also...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: also figuring out how we improve the process.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So if the process is right now,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: lean sale, it's sold, and then goes into a private trust, that we really think of what are those other opportunities

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: that we can take into account, like thinking of abandoned properties or reuse for open space or affordable housing, of course, is one that everyone's talked about.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So that's the, as I said before, that's the remit of really designing it with those questions in mind and those opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How many properties do you have any sense might be eligible in the next year or so, or is it hard to tell?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Oh, it's really hard to tell, especially since we at DEP have also put into place

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: new kind of, not new, but thinking about homeowners and water and sewer bills that we need to collect on, really thinking about how to be more sensitive to the homeowner.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So we've activated things like going out and doing more door knocking, speaking to the homeowner, trying to get them into our affordability programs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: We've increased our affordability programs and expanded them this year.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: So we're, on the one hand, trying to make sure that maybe a homeowner never gets to that point, and so we can't really predict which ones or how many would go into it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you, and congratulations on your Daily News editorial topic today.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Garcia
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Seeing all the members have questions, Commissioner Garcia, your excuse, and we also are joined by Council Member Lee.

chapters.summary: Ung introduces the nomination of Dr. Dave Chokshi to the Board of Health, explains the board's role in legislating the NYC Health Code, and notes members serve six-year terms without pay and cannot be dismissed without cause.
chapters.title: Chair Ung transitions to Dr. Chokshi nomination and Board of Health overview

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We will now move on to the mayor's nominee for the Board of Health, pursuant to Section 31 and 553 of the Charter, and by the letter dated August 7,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: 2026, the mayor requested the advice and consent of the council regarding the appointment of Dr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Dave Chokshi to the New York City Board of Health.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The appointment will expire on May 31, 2030.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The primary function of the Board of Health is to legislate and oversee the New York City's health code, which encompasses the rules governing all matters and subjects within the jurisdiction of the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The department jurisdiction is among the most extensive and varied of all the city agencies and includes such diverse disciplines as communicable diseases, environmental health services,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: radiological health, food safety, veterinarian affairs, water quality, pest control, and vital statistics, and the Office of Chief Medical Examiner.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The board's health 11 members serve six years term without pay and cannot be dismissed without cause.

chapters.summary: Ung details Chokshi's roles as City College professor, Common Health Coalition chair, former NYC Health Commissioner during COVID-19, former H&H chief population health officer, and White House Fellow under President Obama.
chapters.title: Chair Ung introduces Dr. Chokshi's extensive public health background

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We are joined today by Dr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Dave Chokshi.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Dr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Chakshi is currently the Sternberg Family Professor and founding director of the Health and Opportunity Leadership Institute at the City College of New York.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: He's also the chair of the Common Health Coalition and the co-chair of Health and Political Economy Project.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: From 2020 to 2022, he served as the commissioner of the New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, leading the city's response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: During his tenure, he's also served as the chair of the New York City Board of Health, where he promulgated a resolution recognizing racism as a public health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: He also launched the nation's first publicly authorized overdose prevention centers.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: From 2014 to 2020, he held leadership roles at the New York City Health and Hospitals, including serving as inaugural chief population health officer.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: From 2017 to 2020, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Chakshi is also the Chief Executive Officer of H&H Accountable Care Organization and in 2012 was appointed by the President Barack Obama to serve as the White House Fellow at the U.S.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Department of Veteran Affairs where he was a Principal Health Advisor in the Office of the Secretary.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: He received his doctorate from the University of Pennsylvania.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm going to ask Dr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Chokshi to come up to the table.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And now I recognize the committee counsel to administer the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in your statements before this committee and in response to all questions posed by council members?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Chokshi.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I now recognize you to make an opening statement.

chapters.summary: Chokshi describes himself as a primary care doctor with a public health heart, sharing his personal journey as the first doctor in his family, his father's diabetes, and his experience caring for patients at Bellevue Hospital since 2014.
chapters.title: Dr. Chokshi opening statement: personal background and public health career

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Ung and council members.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: It is an honor to be with you today.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: My name is Dave Choksey, and I'm a primary care doctor with a public health heart.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I've cared for patients at Bellevue Hospital since 2014, before, during, and after my service as the 43rd Health Commissioner of New York City, which is how some of you may know me.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: As Commissioner, I had the privilege of chairing the Board of Health, so I come to you with deep respect for the Board and direct knowledge of its vital work on behalf of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Today, my clinical practice focuses on people experiencing homelessness, and I'm a professor at the City College of New York, where I founded the Health and Opportunity Leadership Institute.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I also chair the Common Health Coalition, the largest multi-sector health coalition in the nation.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Across all of it, my career has been dedicated to saving lives and preventing suffering.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: That is why I would be honored to serve again on the Board of Health.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: The board is an historic institution, safeguarding New Yorkers for over two centuries.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: From scourges like smallpox and cholera to present-day diseases,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: like cancer and COVID-19, the board has been at the forefront of public health.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I think of its mission simply.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Adding healthy birthdays for all of us.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: For my part, I came to medicine without early role models.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I am the first doctor in my family.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: But like so many, I learned

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: learn from direct experience how closely health is tied to opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: From being hospitalized with asthma as a child, to watching my father live with diabetes for decades.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Opportunity brought my father from Mumbai to Baton Rouge, where I was born and raised, and my wife's family to Queens, where we are raising our own daughters today.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: My patients remind me of those journeys.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Each deserves excellent care, and each would benefit even more if their illness could be prevented in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: That is the promise of public health.

chapters.summary: Chokshi highlights his tenure as health commissioner, including vaccinating 6 million New Yorkers, launching overdose prevention centers, and passing the racism as public health crisis resolution. He identifies modernizing the health system amid federal funding cuts as the greatest challenge.
chapters.title: Dr. Chokshi opening statement: COVID response, board achievements, and challenges ahead

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Before I came to the health department, I served six years at New York City Health and Hospitals, including as its inaugural chief population health officer.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: As health commissioner during the COVID-19 pandemic, I led our city's historic campaign to vaccinate over 6 million New Yorkers in just over a year.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: During my tenure, the department also launched signature initiatives on overdose prevention, community health workers, and nurse visits for new moms and babies.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And as chair of the Board of Health, I promulgated a landmark resolution on racism as a public health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: The greatest challenge currently facing the board and the department is modernizing our health system in the face of national headwinds for public health.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Federal policy changes and funding cuts have weakened health infrastructure and caused coverage losses here as well as nationally.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Contending with these headwinds will require

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: require creativity, innovation, and attention to low-income and marginalized New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Above all, it will require listening with humility.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Community engagement is a foremost duty in public health, and I strongly believe that it must be a bidirectional conduit.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Health leaders must listen as much as we speak.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: If appointed, I intend to take that duty as seriously as I take listening to my own patients.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I welcome the chance to learn from this council, which has a particularly important role in identifying areas for policymaking.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Mayor Mamdani for this nomination and to Deputy Mayor Arteaga and Commissioner Martin for their confidence.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: It has been a privilege to serve our city in various roles over more than a decade now, and I would look forward to the chance to do so again through the Board of Health.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you for your time, your consideration, and your commitment to our beloved city.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

chapters.summary: Ung asks about specific progress on the 2021 racism resolution. Chokshi explains the resolution required annual reporting and tangible actions, particularly important during COVID-19, and acknowledges the work continues for Black, brown, and Native American New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Chokshi on racism as public health crisis since 2021

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: In October of 2021, when you were the city health commissioner, the Board of Health passed a resolution declaring that racism is a public health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: In what specific ways do you think the Board of Health and Department of Health have been effective in addressing this crisis since 2021?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And what work do you think the Board of Health and the Department of Health still need to do to address this racism in public health in 2026?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you for the thoughtful question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is one of the things that I'm proudest of from my tenure as health commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: We very deliberately called it a resolution on racism as a public health crisis because it requires resolve for us to be able to confront the many ways in which racism

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: contributes to health inequities.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: During the time that we passed that resolution, we put in specific language to ensure that there would be annual reporting that the department was required to make for us to ensure that there were tangible actions being taken.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This was particularly important during the COVID-19 pandemic, of course, where we saw the ways in which the pernicious reach of racism affect the everyday lives of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Since then, the department has continued its focus on equity, but of course the work continues because in so many ways, low income,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Black and brown New Yorkers, Native American New Yorkers continue to face the brunt of inequities and poor health outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Well, you did mention the annual reporting.

chapters.summary: Chokshi elaborates on the need to move from data to action, identifying cardiovascular disease, cancer, severe mental illness, and infectious diseases like hepatitis C and HIV as areas requiring targeted interventions for marginalized communities.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Chokshi on annual reporting and translating data to action

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Was there some, you know, in this annual report, could you further just elaborate on that and what else we can do?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I think that one of the things that is most important with respect to what has to be done going forward is for us to take the data

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: that the department is excellent at producing and moving from data to action.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: For us to identify the most concrete ways for whether it's physical health or mental health or substance use,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: ways for us to take that data and translate it into interventions that can close those gaps.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: So, for example, I think we have to continue to look at ways in which cardiovascular disease, cancer,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: severe mental illness, and infectious diseases like hepatitis C and HIV are born particularly by

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: racial minorities and other New Yorkers who are marginalized.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: There are specific interventions that we can continue to elaborate to be able to meet those challenges.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Chokshi states the Board of Health is ultimately accountable to the public, noting its six-year terms are designed to insulate decisions from political currents so scientific merit and public responsiveness guide outcomes.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Chokshi on board accountability to the public

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: As the Board of Health member, to whom do you believe you're ultimately accountable?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The mayor, the commissioner of health, or the public, and why?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: The Board of Health is ultimately accountable to the public.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I feel a great deal of humility with respect to the role of the Board of Health because it is such a historic institution.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: For almost 200 years, it has served the public.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And the board, as I'm sure you know, Chair, is specifically designed with its six-year terms to be

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: somewhat insulated from the political currents of the day so that responsiveness to the public and scientific merit are the key considerations by which its decisions are made.

chapters.summary: Chokshi describes the Council-Board relationship as important, noting Council represents the people and should communicate with the Board about health code amendments responsive to public priorities.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Chokshi on Council's role with Board of Health

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And what role do you think the City Council should play in overseeing the Board of Health?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I see the relationship between the Board of Health and City Council as a particularly important one.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: City Council, of course, represents

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: the people of New York City as well.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And so when it comes to policies that should be identified, there are avenues that City Council, of course, has purview

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: over itself, but there may be ways in which the health code ought to be amended to be responsive to

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: public priorities.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And so in those cases, the city council and the board of health should communicate and work together with respect to any changes to the health code.

chapters.summary: Ung asks how Chokshi would respond if data showed policies weren't working. Chokshi emphasizes data is the lifeblood of public health and adjustments must be made when intended aims aren't achieved.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Chokshi on data-driven policy adjustment

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So we were just talking about data.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So how will you respond if the data suggested that the board policy was not achieving its intended public health outcomes?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: That's another thoughtful question.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: We always have to adjust when the data shows that we are not achieving our intended aims.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This also requires humility alongside public accountability, but it's one of the things that I love the most about public health because data is in our DNA.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: You know, we believe that data is the lifeblood of what we do in public health, not just because it identifies priorities for action, but because

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: within it is also accountability to make sure that we're actually serving the people that we intend to serve as well as possible.

chapters.summary: Chokshi discusses mechanisms for public input including written comments and oral testimony, and states that if a board policy produced unintended negative consequences, the primary responsibility is to adjust the approach.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Chokshi on self-evaluation and unintended consequences

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And how will you evaluate your own performance as a member of the board?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Well, I think, again, that is ultimately up to the public, you know, to evaluate.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I can say some of the ways in which I will hold with great gravity

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: my own role on the Board of Health, and that is to ensure that the things that we're doing are responsive to public input and feedback.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: As you know, there are mechanisms to ensure that.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: public input to the Board of Health, whether the written comments, you know, before rulemaking or the ways in which meetings of the Board of Health are public and there are ways for oral testimony by members of the public to be given.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And so I think those will be the most important mechanisms for us to understand whether the board is truly responding to public health needs.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And if the board adopted a policy that produced unintended negative consequences, what is the responsibility that the board member should bear?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: The responsibility primarily is to adjust, you know, to ensure that if things are not going as is intended, that the board adjusts its approach.

chapters.summary: Chokshi emphasizes existing mechanisms for public accountability through written comments and public testimony at Board of Health meetings as the most important channels for incorporating community feedback.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Chokshi on responding to community stakeholder concerns

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And if the community stakeholders raise concerns about a board action, how do you respond and incorporate their feedback?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is another very important part of how the Board of Health remains publicly accountable.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: As I briefly alluded to earlier, you know, there are existing mechanisms through written public comments as well as public testimony during Board of Health meetings.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Those are the most important mechanisms to ensure public accountability.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I would like now to pass it off to Councilmember Krishnan.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks about the health impacts of heavy screen use on children. Chokshi acknowledges growing evidence of mental health harms and opportunity costs to physical activity and sleep, noting enough evidence exists to act on limiting screen time while monitoring emerging research.
chapters.title: CM Krishnan Q&A: Chokshi on screens and social media as public health issue

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Chokshi, City's doctor.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Those COVID commercials are ingrained in my head from before.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I'm glad to be not on your TV anymore, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Still, public health works.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Look at that.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So I still remember it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But it's good to see you, Doctor, and thank you for all your work during some of the most difficult parts of our city's recent history when it came to public health.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I have seen all that you've done, too, and also appreciate that you're representing my district proudly in all that you do across the city.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I just had a couple of quick questions.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: One is pretty specific, and I wanted to get your thoughts on it, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In a few weeks, my committee will be holding a hearing around an issue that's really of concern to me, which is around the heavy reliance of schools on screens,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: the heavy reliance on screens in schools, especially for young children.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And as a father of young children myself, I see how much of an issue that is.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And it kind of goes from there to social media and the harmful impacts of social media.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And we've, with the Youth Committee, too, held a hearing on that earlier this year.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And of course there are other questions that come in with the use of AI and even unknowingly children's exposure to AI through some of the programs that are used in schools.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so I bring all of that up to say.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You know, I think.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: that screens for this generation and for young children in particular is becoming a real concern from a policy standpoint across our society, frankly, and especially in our country.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And to me, it raises the question of it's reached the point where it's a public health issue, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's a mental health concern, especially as kids get older.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And, you know, more broadly speaking, it is a public health issue.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so I just wonder how you think about that, how you think in this position on the board, you would think about the issue of screens and the overuse of screens when it comes to children, especially young children.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is a really thoughtful question and an area where there's active debate about what precisely needs to be done.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I'll offer some of my thoughts, but I first do want to ensure that I state that the Board of Health may have limited purview over this issue just by virtue of

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: the fact that it may not require health code changes, but may require other mechanisms, you know, by which either the Department of Health or other aspects of city government are responsible for it.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: So I do want to represent that aspect.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: But I can share, speaking as a doctor, but also as the father of two young girls, this is very concerning to me.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: There is growing evidence that there are harms related to mental health from exposure to devices, you know, not just the screens component.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: of it, but some of the other ways in which technology can affect mental health, both for very young children, but also for teenagers and adolescents.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: The other aspect that I think is very concerning is beyond mental health, although that is the primary reason for concern, there's an opportunity cost with respect to what

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: kids are doing when they are spending so much time on screens.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: What is it coming at the expense of, particularly physical activity or sleep, which is also very important, you know, for the health of developing brains and developing bodies.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: So those are all things that I think we have to take very seriously and monitor the evidence as it emerges.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I think we have enough evidence to act in some ways with respect to limiting screen time and the use of devices.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And then I think we have to continue, you know, monitoring the evidence base to understand what additional steps need to be taken.

chapters.summary: Krishnan raises concerns about the healthcare system's focus on reactive care over prevention, especially affecting low-income communities of color. Chokshi agrees, citing his career dedication to primary care and public health prevention, and commits to looking upstream at root causes.
chapters.title: CM Krishnan Q&A: Chokshi on prevention vs reactive medicine

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And perhaps there are ways that, while not all of it is in your jurisdiction, but there are ways that we could work together to think about larger awareness campaigns around it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: My final question, just zooming out, you know, apart from your nomination too, but more broadly,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: you know, one of the things that troubles me a lot is aside from healthcare becoming more and more unaffordable, insurance premiums going up, services being cut to allow, you know, billion-dollar insurance companies to further profit.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's all stemming from a view that I'm seeing in medicine more and more of reactive care, where once someone gets sick or has a heart attack, there's a battery of tests, you're coded a certain way

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: under insurance company rules.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But before that, from a prevention standpoint, it's often very difficult to get the care that you need.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And that care really starts, as you know, a lot earlier, years before a health incident can happen.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But we don't focus enough on prevention in medicine, and that's driven a lot by insurance companies and larger profit measures and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And, you know, I think that the lack of focus on prevention really affects low-income communities of color especially.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I think you speak about it too when you talk about racism in the context of public health.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: These are all connected.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so when we don't reach out and really inform people of the importance of prevention and offer preventative services, the disparate harms of that are felt by low-income communities of color.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so I just wonder, you know, in your role in the Board of Health, as we think about community engagement and outreach too, how can the board work to help?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In its own way, shift perspective from reactive medicine to preventative care.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: That's really well said, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you for shining a light on that.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I've dedicated

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: my career to primary care and public health, which both have prevention at their heart.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And it troubles me also the degree to which the money does not follow that paradigm of investing in prevention.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And so that is, you know, a posture, a viewpoint that I will bring to deliberations on the Board of Health to ensure that prevention remains at the center,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: that we, as we sometimes say in medicine, look upstream, not just to the reasons that someone comes with illness-seeking care, but the deeper, you know, causes.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: That underlie that illness in the first place.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And all of that, I believe, is the remit of public health.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And now I'd like to pass it over to the majority of your aburial.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks about the board's role in eliminating childhood lead poisoning. Chokshi notes the board historically amended the health code to remove interior lead paint and says the agency takes the threat seriously, though he's not aware of current needed code changes.
chapters.title: CM Abreu Q&A: Chokshi on childhood lead poisoning

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and thank you, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Chokshi, for your previous service to our city and for your continued interest.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In public service to our city.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I have questions on childhood poisoning and vaccinations.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What is the board's health's role in eliminating child-led poisoning, and do you believe changes to the health code are needed to address this problem?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is another critically important issue.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: As you likely know, the Board of Health was the body that first called attention to and amended the health code to remove interior

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: lead paint from New York City buildings and particularly from our homes and schools.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And so I believe the board certainly has an important role to play when it comes to ensuring that lead poisoning is something that no child in New York City should ever be exposed to.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: To your specific question, I'm not aware of current regulations or current changes to the health code that are needed to advance the work that has already happened, but I do know intimately that

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: the agency takes this very seriously as a threat to childhood health.

chapters.summary: Chokshi expresses concern about falling vaccination rates, noting measles, mumps, rubella, and polio are preventable tragedies. He emphasizes the importance of trusted messengers, particularly pediatricians and community health workers, over government officials alone.
chapters.title: CM Abreu Q&A: Chokshi on falling vaccination rates and misinformation

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As a Board of Health member, how would you address failing, sorry, how would you address falling vaccination rates and combat vaccine misinformation?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is something that I'm also very concerned about, so thank you for spotlighting it as well.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: We have work to do with respect to

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: trust with respect to contending with misinformation, most importantly with ensuring that children are protected against what are completely preventable illnesses.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Every single case of measles, of

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: mumps, rubella, polio, these are preventable tragedies with vaccination.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: So the things that we have to do, number one,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: We have to ensure that it is not just about the messages that we're delivering about vaccination, but also the messengers.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is something that we took seriously during the pandemic for the health department to know when it was time for government officials to take a step back and to empower others, whether it was community health workers or faith leaders,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: to engage in that type of conversation.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: The people who remain the most trusted by members of the public, by patients and parents, are people's own doctors.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
