utterances.text: And so I think there's an important role to ensure engagement, particularly of pediatricians, to ensure that the best evidence-based information is transmitted to people.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Great.

chapters.summary: Abreu asks about AI's potential role in public health. Chokshi acknowledges both potential harms from technology and potential benefits for improving access to care, advocating for a level-headed appreciation of both.
chapters.title: CM Abreu Q&A: Chokshi on AI in public health

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Now I have two set of questions on artificial intelligence.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: What are some specific ways you see the Board of Health and the health department potentially using AI to impact public health outcomes and public health education?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is something that I have been thinking about.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Again, I will sort of check the responsibilities of the Board of Health to say that I'm not aware of any current ways in which that will intersect with the Board of Health's jurisdiction or with amendments to the health code.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: With that said, speaking as a doctor and public health professional myself, I think we have to hold in our hands both the idea that AI and technology

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: you know, to the prior question, could have some health harms that we need to be cognizant of, but also that there may be some ways in which using artificial intelligence could improve access to care

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: or help us ensure delivery of care to people who most need it.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: So I think we have to have a level-headed appreciation of both the harms and the potential benefits.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Well, you answered my question on the harms, so that eliminates that second question.

chapters.summary: Chokshi discusses the challenge of federal policy changes and funding cuts weakening public health infrastructure. He emphasizes first doing no harm, partnering with the state, and improving collaboration between public health and healthcare sectors through the Common Health Coalition.
chapters.title: CM Abreu Q&A: Chokshi on modernizing health system amid federal cuts

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My final question, it's on your, in your pre-hearing questions, you were asked about what you envision to be the greatest challenge facing the Board of Health and Department of Health in the next five years.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You stated that the greatest

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Such challenge is, quote, modernizing our health system in the face of headwinds for public health at the national level, unquote.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You further stated, quote, federal policy changes and funding cuts have resulted in a weakened public health infrastructure and health coverage losses nationally as well in New York City, unquote.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How do you envision the Board of Health and Department of Health being able to address these particular challenges that you have identified?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is something that I am very concerned about, and I know members of the Council are as well.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I also would commend the department, including the current leadership, for paying deep attention to these issues.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I think what has to be done, first and foremost, is what we talk about in medicine, to

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: first do no harm, you know, to ensure that the changes as they come down are mitigated to the degree possible

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: through city actions and potentially partnership with the state as well when it comes to people who may be losing their health coverage, whether it's Medicaid or an Affordable Care Act plan.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Beyond that, I think that the ways in which funding cuts are being borne means that we have to get more creative with respect to our public health infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Something that I feel very passionately about is the ways in which public health and health care

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: ought to partner better together.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is why I helped to co-found the Common Health Coalition to make it so that all sectors of health, hospitals, health plans,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: health departments are pushing in the same direction for the most urgent health priorities, and frankly, so that patients shouldn't have to think that much about what branch of the health system they are interacting with

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: and say that that is a responsibility that is borne by us as health professionals on the back end.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you so much, doctor.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We missed you on the commercials.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I'm done with my questions.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Lee expresses deep appreciation for Chokshi's all-community approach to health, recalling their partnership at Korean Community Services on hepatitis B, diabetes, and healthy food initiatives. She notes he understood diverse health needs better than previous commissioners.
chapters.title: CM Lee: appreciation for Chokshi's community health approach

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'd like now to pass it on to Councilmember Lee.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Oh my gosh, I almost spilled my coffee, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Hi, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Chokshi, how are you?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Hi, I'm doing well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: I just want to start off by saying, it's more comments than questions, but I just want to say I have a huge amount of respect, and I just wanted to thank you so much, because during COVID and even before that, I was the executive director at Korean Community Services.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I remember.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Yes, and I just love your all-community approach to health, because that is what it takes, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And even when we were at KCS, I remember being outside the steps of City Hall saying, no, hepatitis B and C and diabetes are huge issues in our community, but there was no data at the time or not enough data in our communities.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so that's why we partnered a lot and did the community-based participatory research and worked with H-Mark Grocery Store to get the healthy aisle, you know, food items at eye level, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And the restaurants in K-Town to do low-sodium options and the faith-based leaders to really do screenings at the churches.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And it takes a village, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And so I just want to say I really, really appreciate your approach to health because it is public health.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: It is an all-inclusive sort of effort.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I just wanted to say thank you in all of your many roles and hats that you've worn because I did have previous health commissioners, not you, who sort of didn't understand or appreciate the diverse health needs of our city.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I think you brought that to the table.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And I just wanted to say thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Lee asks how the board can partner with city agencies for multilingual outreach amid threats like public charge and HR1. Chokshi cites his pride in releasing the first AAPI health report and the importance of disaggregated data, and points to NYC Care as a safety net for coverage losses.
chapters.title: CM Lee Q&A: Chokshi on outreach, coverage, and public charge concerns

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And just, I guess, in my former role in HAT.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: that I'm putting on a little bit, you know, given, I guess, your previous background and what's happening and coming down the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Because as you just mentioned, a lot of times it's not your health issues necessarily that dictate what kind of services you have.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: It's the health insurance and what type of coverage you have that dictates what kind of

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: services we are able to receive, which is kind of backwards, right?

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And it's not enough on prevention.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And we all know that preventive care, you know, saves the city and state dollars and also keeps us healthier.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: But given everything that's changing in the political landscape, how do you think

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: given public charge, what we saw last time, and HR1 and everything, how will your role on the board

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: sort of partner with other city agencies to help make sure that we are doing the outreach in multiple languages into the community so that everyone knows their rights and we keep people healthy?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Well, first of all, thank you so much for the kind words, Councilmember Lee.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: It means a lot to me coming from you.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I do have to mention I'm very proud of being the first health commissioner of Asian descent in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And as part of that, even as busy as it was during the pandemic, one of my proudest achievements was releasing the first ever report on the health of Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders for New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And I think that gets to your question as well, because it starts with our ability.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: to disaggregate data so that we can actually see what is happening in this, you know, the beautiful mosaic, as it's called here in New York City,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: and understand what the health problems are that are being contended with in different communities so that we can be responsive to them.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I'm also worried about some of the political headwinds, you know, that you have described and the way that they will affect the health of particularly low-income and marginalized New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And the one thing that I will just say briefly on that is that, you know, I'm proud to have been a part of New York City Health and Hospitals as well, and I think that H&H has done terrific work when it comes to NYC Care,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: and I know it's very much on their radar screen to think about how NYC Care can rise to the challenge of what we're confronting and will continue to over the coming months when it comes to those coverage losses.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: And the partners on the ground, and especially those that do public health or mental health-related work in the community, they're ready to go.

utterances.speaker: Linda Lee
utterances.text: So I would say definitely let's partner with them, too.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about Chokshi's focus as a physician member, animal issues under Board of Health purview, drug overdoses, and mental health crises including problems with 988. Chokshi addresses each topic, emphasizing naloxone access, medication-assisted treatment, youth mental health, and lowering barriers to care.
chapters.title: CM Brewer Q&A: Chokshi on physician role, animals, drugs, and mental health

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And I would like to now pass it off to Council Member Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I too remember the ads.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So you are famous for the taxi radio television thing, whatever it was.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: First is just to get, I think there are obviously other doctors from health and H&H on the board, but I believe you would be the doctor appointed physician.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: That would be one of your roles.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question would be kind of what would be some of your focus points that you would like to achieve?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number two, unfortunately, animals are often under your purview, Board of Health.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have been to the Board of Health so many times, animal issues, the nine to nine even in the parks comes under the Board of Health.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I just wanted to think, because unfortunately there are so many challenges in terms of the animal world that we're dealing with.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I want to know your comments on that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And also drug.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: challenges.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We have too many people dying of drugs, different types, coming somewhat under the board, maybe in terms of policies that could be changed.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then just Linda Lee and I all often focus on the mental health.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have to say, I've called 988 a couple of times recently, has been not helpful at all.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so mental health is just not working.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So those would be my three questions.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you for all the ways that you have supported and uplifted the health of New Yorkers over the years.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Too many.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: You covered a lot of ground there.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Let me try to get briefly to each of them.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: With respect to the physicians on the Board of Health, as you likely know, statutorily there are specific slots for physicians.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: The chair, of course, is the current commissioner, Commissioner Martin, who is a doctor.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Dr.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Katz is also a member of the Board of Health, the current CEO of Health and Hospitals, and I would be another one of the physician members.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I think it is important to have physicians, particularly practicing physicians, represented on the board.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: With respect to animals, drugs, and mental health, you're absolutely right that animals,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: the way in which veterinary medicine interacts with human health, but also some of the specific policy issues related to animals in New York City comes under the board's purview.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: There aren't any specific sort of issues that I'm aware will be brought before the board in the near term.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: So what I can say is that that is an area that as health commissioner, you know, I also had purview over, and so I have expertise in, and I also know where in the literature to look for the latest scientific evidence to help evaluate those questions.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: For substance use, this is again an area where I am very concerned.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: As you said, we lose too many of our fellow New Yorkers to overdose.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: There are some things that have been done, particularly over the last several years, to try to change that.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I think the pillars of the approach are, number one, ensure that we do everything that we can to keep our fellow New Yorkers alive so that they can seek treatment and rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: For example, making naloxone more accessible.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And then second, we have to expand our efforts around medication-assisted treatment to ensure that people actually get treated and can enter into rehabilitation.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And then number three, and I should say not all of these will intersect with the Board of Health, but number three is being very vigilant with respect to how the drug supply is changing.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is something that nationally is causing huge problems because synthetic versions of various drugs are extremely dangerous for...

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: You know, for a, for a,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: people and patients.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: So that's another, you know, aspect of the approach.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And then finally, with respect to mental health, you know, I think there are two things that I have to say about that.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: One is to arc back to the prior part of the conversation, focusing on young people in particular.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is where so much of the groundwork is laid for our health in adulthood.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And the more that we can do to address mental health of young people, the more dividends it will pay over time.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And then second is to ensure greater access.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: You know, we have NYC Well in addition to 988.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: But I take your point that there are ways that we can continue to lower barriers to accessing mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, not to push it, but 9 and 8 didn't help two individuals that I'm trying to help right now.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Not at all, didn't refer, didn't anything.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And also, just back to the animals for a second, I mean, it's overcrowding is a huge issue.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: We could go on and on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I just think it pops up in the press even more than some of the other issues that might be more important.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But I think that more attention needs to be paid to that.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And then just in terms of the coordination, which is good, because I think the Board of Health is one of the few places where H&H and Health Department can work together on some of their policies.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is that something that you think could be extended or could be dealt with better?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: The short answer is yes, although I'll answer with

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: humility, you know, the current leaders of those agencies.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: They're terrific.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: They're wonderful.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: They're primary.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I'm a big Dr.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Katz fan.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: As am I.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And I'd like to pass it off to Minority Leader Carr.

chapters.summary: Carr asks Chokshi to reflect on COVID decisions with hindsight. Chokshi acknowledges the loss of nearly 50,000 New Yorkers and says he would have paid more attention to how variants change and communicated that more nimbly to the public.
chapters.title: Minority Leader Carr Q&A: Chokshi on COVID pandemic regrets

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Ong.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Doctor, good to see you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you for being here today.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I want to talk to you a little bit about the response to the COVID pandemic, during which you were a major policymaker, advisor, leader for the city of New York.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Looking back on that time now,

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: with the benefit of hindsight, is there anything that you would do differently or anything specifically that you regret in terms of decisions or recommendations made at that time?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you, Leader Carr, for the question.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And, you know, I have to start by saying when I look back on that time, there's a lot of pain and tragedy and suffering that we have to acknowledge.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: We lost almost 50,000 of our fellow New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Of course, not numbers.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: You know, they were our neighbors, our family members, our friends.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And that's something that I think we have to acknowledge with, you know, with gravity.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: There are so many ways in which I believe that the city

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: and everyday people rose to the occasion, you know, with respect to saving lives and preventing suffering, whether it was from, you know, the way that people made sure that older adults had what they needed, you know,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: in those early weeks.

chapters.summary: Carr presses on whether the city worker vaccine mandate was justified given CDC findings it didn't stop transmission. Chokshi defends the mandate, noting the vaccine reduces transmission risk and prevents hospitalizations and deaths. Carr argues terminated workers deserve their jobs back; Chokshi says that's a matter for the current administration.
chapters.title: Minority Leader Carr Q&A: Chokshi on vaccine mandate justification

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: of the pandemic, bringing them food and groceries, to the way that the vaccination campaign ultimately saved tens of thousands of lives.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: But you asked if there was anything that might be done differently in retrospect.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And I think one thing that comes to mind for me is the way in which the virus changed so quickly.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: We encountered different variants of the virus that causes COVID-19, and that shifted the way that we had to respond to it.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And so looking back, I think I would have paid even more attention to the ways in which variants can arise, communicated that to the public.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And made sure that we were as nimble as possible because from Alpha to Delta to Omicron, it required slightly different responses of our city.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I join you in remembering the weight of the loss of those tens of thousands of New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And I think what I hear from mostly from folks looking back now is also the financial pain that that

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: period brought the lockdowns as well as the mandates and in particular folks who worked in service to the city who no longer do so because of a vaccine mandate

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: a vaccine mandate that after your tenure as commissioner the CDC published reports saying that it did not actually do anything to stop the spread it certainly contains symptoms I got vaccinated

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: vaccinated myself, I was happy to make that choice.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But that choice was stripped away from many, many, many city workers who still are fighting to get their jobs back.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So in light of what the CDC said after your tenure as commissioner, is that mandate a decision that you regret being supportive of?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that the vaccination campaign unequivocally saved lives and prevented suffering.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I'm proud of the fact that we were able to vaccinate over 6 million New Yorkers in a little bit over a year.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And I would say that that required an all hands on deck approach.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: You know, I'm proud that New York City was the first major municipality to lower barriers to accessing the vaccine as far as possible.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: We were the first place that brought vaccines in people's homes, you know, to ensure that everyone who wanted a vaccine could get one.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: We invested tens of millions of dollars in community health workers.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: It was the largest city community health worker program to ensure that people could get their questions answered about the COVID-19 vaccine, which all of the science indicates was safe and effective.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And I do believe that the judicious use of vaccine requirements is something that has to stay in the remit of public health, whether it's

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: vaccine requirements that help our children stay safe in schools or the vaccine requirements that were associated with a once-in-a-generation pandemic?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I think that the issue isn't whether the government should have this power.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: The question is whether or not it was used judiciously and correctly in the moment that you were talking about right now.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I think reducing barriers to the vaccine, promoting accessibility, promoting education and information, those are all great things.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I think for the most part, most people should have taken the vaccine.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But ultimately, given that what we know about what was said at the time, which is that this is going to stop the spread, which turned out to not be true.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So it was clearly just a question of a person's individual public, individual health, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: There was no reason for there to have been a mandate.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And many of those people who chose to be severed from city service and were wrongfully terminated, in my view, are still with us.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: They did not succumb to the future variants of the illness.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So they made the correct health bet, but it's cost them in terms of their career and their livelihood.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And so I'm asking you, do you really feel like that that was worth it?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Do you feel like that was the correct decision?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: In spite of the fact that the city did not have to surrender its policymaking ability to impose such a mandate in the future.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Yes, and I do understand your perspective.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I will clarify that the best scientific evidence indicates that

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Although the vaccine may not completely stop the spread of the virus, it does reduce the risk of transmission.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And that was true even for subsequent variants of the virus.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: And perhaps even more importantly, with respect to being able to prevent hospitalizations and deaths, that is absolutely well-founded and supported by evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Do you believe that the folks who are looking to return to their jobs at their previous pay and seniority should be allowed to do so at this point?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I believe that that's a matter for the current administration and for the current decision makers.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: All I can say is for the decisions that were made during that extraordinarily difficult time, I do stand by them.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I think unfortunately in retrospect it turned out to not be the right call and I think a lot of these folks deserve to be able to return to their jobs.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: They were great city workers before and we need good city workers on the city payroll and the workforce.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So we just disagree on this one, but thank you for your candor and thank you chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Epstein asks about the hospital system's role in moving homeless people to housing and the changes to involuntary commitment law. Chokshi praises Bridge to Home and SHOW vans, and argues the real solution is expanding transitional and supportive housing supply and intensive community treatment teams rather than involuntary commitment.
chapters.title: CM Epstein Q&A: Chokshi on homelessness, supportive housing, and involuntary commitment

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: You're also joined by Council Member Epstein, who also has a few questions.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you for your time.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I want to just turn our attention to the homeless crisis that we experience in New York City and kind of the role that the hospital system plays in helping people move into housing and supportive housing.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do you see the hospital system as a key infrastructure for people with mental health issues, Bridge to Home, which is at Bellevue?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And what do you think your role is to ensure we get people from the streets into supportive housing in more organized settings?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you for the thoughtful question.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I'll again start by just sort of checking my own responsibility as a potential Board of Health member.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: It's limited with respect to the role of the hospital system, you know, particularly health and hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: With that said, Councilmember, this is something that I'm personally very passionate about.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: As you may have heard, I practice at Bellevue, and my practice focuses on people experiencing homelessness.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I've taken care of several patients who have benefited from Bridge to Home.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I think it's an excellent model, and I believe that what H&H has done, particularly over the last several years, to

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: advance both health care for people experiencing homelessness and then connect people to housing is unequivocally something that benefits their health.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: So I'm supportive of that, and I think that as we...

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: continue to elaborate additional interventions of that type of category, it will benefit New Yorkers who are homeless.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: And the second question just around, like, I understand, you know, since you've practiced at Bellevue, there's a large conversation about whether someone should be involuntarily committed or not, the changes in the state law from two years ago.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Do you think that our H&H system and your role, are we doing a good enough job identifying people with serious mental health issues,

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: using the changes in the law that talk about people being able to take care of their basic needs and ensuring that those people are getting the support they need?

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Because we've seen this cycle of people going in and out of specifically Bellevue and other H&H facilities and then unfortunately doing harm to themselves or to others, even though they're well known to the H&H system.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: This is a challenging issue, and I can say clinically it's something that you have to use very judiciously, you know, to ensure that

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: people's rights are protected, even as you are trying to protect their health, you know, at the same time.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: My perspective is that the major sort of intervention, the solution, is actually on the other end, what we were talking about earlier, ensuring that there are pathways for transitional housing,

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: ensuring that barriers to supportive housing and the supply of supportive housing

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: are sufficient.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Making sure that people with serious mental illness have access to the ACT and IMT and other intensive mobile treatment teams in the community.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: So I think those are where I think the greatest focus should be placed.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: I said I didn't have one more question, but I do have one more if I can.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: So you would expand programs like SHOW or other mobile-based programs to get people to have access to services?

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: The short answer is yes, but I have to acknowledge my conflict of interest.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: I practice on the show vans myself, and so it would be difficult for me to say anything other than that.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Harvey D. Epstein
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And seeing no other members who have questions, Dr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Chakshi, you are excused.

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ung explains the BSA's five-member structure, borough residency limits, and the chair's required professional qualifications as a planner, architect, or engineer with at least 10 years of experience. The appointment expires October 6, 2027.
chapters.title: Chair Ung: BSA structure and charter requirements for chair

utterances.speaker: Dave A. Chokshi
utterances.text: Do I have to gavel back in or no?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay, so pursuant to Section 31 of the Charter and by the letter dated August 7, 2026, the Mayor requested the advice and consent of the Council

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: regarding the appointment of John Manchin to the New York Board of Standards Appeals as its Chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The appointment will expire October 6, 2027.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Section 659 of the Charter states that the BSA must be comprised of five members and no more than two members shall be residents of any one borough.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The charter provides the chair of the BSA must either be a planner with the professional qualification and at least 10 years experience as a planner,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: or a registered architect with at least 10 years experience as an architect, or a licensed professional engineer with at least 10 years experience as an engineer.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The mayor may move the chair for calls after notice and an opportunity to be heard.

chapters.summary: Ung details BSA's role in hearing appeals on zoning and construction code interpretations by DOB and fire code by FDNY, granting variances for unique hardships, and issuing special permits for deviations from zoning requirements.
chapters.title: Chair Ung: BSA powers as administrative appeals body and quasi-judicial entity

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The BSA is an independent board created to decide, request, and resolve disputes about zoning and land use issues.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The BSA helps to uphold the constitutionality of the zoning resolution and the rights of New Yorkers by serving as a relief valve for properties that are uniquely restricted by zoning and land use rules.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: issuing decisions that consider the needs of both the owners and the neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The board is also charged with interpreting decisions of certain land use enforcement agencies, including the Department of Buildings and Fire Department, ensuring that these agencies correctly apply the city's zoning, construction, and fire codes.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Under the city charter, the BSA has a broad set of powers.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: One of the primary responsibilities of the BSA is to act as an administrative appeals body in a quasi-judicial capacity when a property owner, community member, or other interested party

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: disagrees with interpretation, the application of the zoning and resolution.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Or construction codes by city official, usually from the Department of Buildings.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The board is also empowered to hear appeals regarding the application and interpretation of the fire code by FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Another equally important power to BSA is to grant zoning variances.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The variances allow property owners to deviate from the requirements of the zoning resolution on a case-by-case basis where it's proven

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: that the property faces unique hardship that precludes owners from earning a reasonable economic return if developed in strict compliance with the zoning regulations.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The criteria for variances are spelled out in the zoning resolution.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: BSA's council issues special permits.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Like variances, special permits allow a property owner to deviate from the requirements of the zoning resolution.

chapters.summary: Ung explains the 2025 Charter Amendments gave BSA broad powers to approve affordable housing projects that would otherwise violate zoning regulations, previously requiring full ULURP approval through City Planning and City Council. She notes the Council has no formal role in BSA proceedings.
chapters.title: Chair Ung: BSA's expanded affordable housing powers under 2025 Charter Amendments

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: In addition, under the Doherty recently

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Granted to the BSA in the 2025 Charter Amendments, the BSA now has broad powers to allow construction of buildings are to be developed, preserved, or converted in whole and part for affordable housing,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: where these projects will otherwise violate the zoning resolutions used, bulk of parking regulations.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Prior to adoption of the 2025 Charter Amendments, projects such as these will most instances require full yearly approval that would be decided by City Planning Council.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And City Council.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The BSA also has various other powers, including the power to appoint an executive director, the power to issue rules and regulations regarding BSA procedures, public notice to community members, and certain labor law requirements.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The Council has no formal role in the BSA proceedings or in the BSA decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The BSA is legally required to allow public input, but has no real legal obligations to reach any particular outcome based on that input.

chapters.summary: Ung details Mangin's role as DCP Housing Division Director since 2014, his leadership on City of Yes for Housing Opportunity, MIH, and neighborhood plans, his work on the 2025 Charter Revision Commission that reduced council land use powers, and his Yale Law School degree.

utterances.text: In that role, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Manchin led the development of the City of Yes for housing opportunity at Citywide Rezoning that passed in the late 2024.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: He also helped the mandatory inclusion housing and neighborhood plans across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And he has a leadership role in many of the city's other housing and land use initiatives over the past decade.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Manchin also serves as a director of policy and research for the 2025 Charter Revision Commission, which proposed the most significant changes to the city land use review process since 1989.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The resulting charter changes stripped away or reduced many of the council's land use powers.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: The charter changes also enlarged the BSA powers to green light housing projects that do not comply with zoning restrictions.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Before joining the city government, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Manchin worked on a fair housing policy and litigation at the Fair Share Housing in New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: He's also adjunct associate professor at the Urban Planning at NYU Wagner Graduate School of Public Service and a graduate of Yale Law School.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Since we already did the affirmation, I'm going to end.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Ask the candidate for your opening statement.

chapters.summary: Mangin describes his career from working with community groups across NYC after law school, to Fair Share Housing in New Jersey rooted in the Mount Laurel fair housing rulings, emphasizing his commitment to ensuring all people have a voice in land use decisions.
chapters.title: Mangin opening statement: career supporting community participation in land use

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Ung.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Good morning to you and the members of the Committee on Rules, Privileges, Elections, Standards, and Ethics.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm honored to be nominated to be chair of the Board of Standards and Appeals.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The BSA plays a limited but crucial role in the city system of land use regulation.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And if I'm confirmed, I believe I can make that system fairer, more responsive, more transparent, all while supporting affordable housing across the city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I would bring nearly two decades of experience in housing and land use to this role, including creating and preserving

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: affordable housing, handling some of the city's most complex zoning and land use issues, and fostering community participation and land use through direct work with neighborhood groups throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I believe this experience qualifies me for chair of BSA, and I hope to earn your support.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Throughout my career, I've worked to support fairer outcomes by ensuring that all people have a voice in the land use decisions that affect them.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: My first job after law school was working with community groups across the city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: CASA, Fifth Avenue Committee, Community Voices Heard, Good Old Lower East Side, U-House.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: tenants and neighbors, AFI, CHIA CDC, and many, many others to help their communities participate more effectively in land use debates.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Some of those groups were pro-housing, others are anti-development.

chapters.summary: Mangin outlines his 12 years at City Planning working on neighborhood rezonings including SoHo-NoHo, Jamaica, Gowanus, and Midtown South, plus citywide actions like MIH and City of Yes, praising the Council's pro-housing record and role in carrying City of Yes across the finish line.
chapters.title: Mangin opening statement: DCP work on neighborhood rezonings and citywide actions

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That wasn't the point.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The point was improving access and participation.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: This carried over to my work with Fair Share Housing in New Jersey, an organization which grew out of the landmark Mount Laurel Fair Housing rulings in the 70s and 80s.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The Mount Laurel Doctrine recognizes that decisions made by suburbs have consequences for a far broader circle of New Jersey residents whose voices and interests should not be excluded from those decisions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: There, I worked to develop affordable rental and homeownership projects in areas of the state with great schools, access to open space, and other amenities that we all deserve.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I've also carried the spirit of this work through my 12 years at the Department of City Planning.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's included neighborhood rezonings, Soho-Noho, Jamaica, Gowanus, AIMUP, LIC, Midtown South, Jerome Avenue, and many others.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Where city planning went site by site with stakeholders to map out a new future for a neighborhood and partnered with individual council members and local communities on historic packages of capital.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: improvements and other community benefits to support that new housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In this work, I've had the pleasure of working with faith-based organizations across the city, local civic groups, community boards, and many more groups to identify those local needs and opportunities.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That work at City Planning also includes citywide actions, including mandatory inclusionary housing, zoning for quality and affordability, and leading City of Yes for housing opportunity.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I believe that, among other things, City of Yes was the best, most inclusive conversation about housing that this city has ever had.

chapters.summary: Mangin proactively addresses his 2014 article arguing for more housing of all types, noting the argument has since become mainstream. He commits to openness, transparency, and by-the-book compliance at BSA, and expresses excitement about the BSA Fast Track for affordable housing.
chapters.title: Mangin opening statement: addressing 2014 article and BSA fast track goals

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It was a conversation about neighborhoods, but in the context of the broader city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That conversation laid the groundwork for the biggest move on housing in city history and the biggest ever capital investment package to support it.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: When its prospects looked especially grim, the city council, you picked it up and you carried it across the finish line, even though we all realized that politics offered a far easier off-ramp.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm eternally grateful for that, and the city is very much in your debt.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And that's just one example of the council's pro-housing work that I've seen firsthand.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I've seen many of you navigate the complex dynamics and needs of your neighborhoods to make new housing that work.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: for everyone, and I've been proud to partner with you on that work over the last decade.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We all know we have a long way to go to meet the housing needs of our fellow residents, but the significant progress we've made to this point would not be possible without you, the council.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Of course, the BSA does not conduct massive citywide planning efforts like these.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It addresses individual sites such as schools, houses of worship, and healthcare facilities to make projects work to the benefit of landowners, their neighborhoods, and the city at large.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I want to briefly touch on an article I wrote in 2014 that I know some members of the council have asked about.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: At the time I wrote it, I was working in Washington, D.C.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It was the last job I came before I came to New York to work at City Planning.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I was working there with black and Latino tenants and a range of housing advocates.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: To create homeownership cooperative housing under DC's Tenant Opportunity to Purchase Act, TOPA.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: While there, I wrote that article arguing that in addition to all this work that the housing advocates and I were doing, in addition to all those other tools in the community development toolkit,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I felt we should also become forceful advocates for more housing of all types.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Otherwise, it just seemed like we were fighting against the tide.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: At the time, this seemed like a somewhat novel

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: whole argument that we should be in favor of more housing of all types.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Today, I feel like it hardly needs to be said, especially when I look at the council's record on housing over the last decade.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It seems to me like this argument has become a reality.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: At BSA, I will maintain my career-long commitment to openness, transparency, and community voice.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I fully believe that an informed

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: an inclusive process leads to fairer outcomes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I strongly believe that a fair and open process also demands by the book compliance with the laws that guide BSA decisions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: This includes meeting every finding for an approval and recognizing that actions that could affect neighborhood character must go to City Planning Commission and the City Council.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: At BSA, I would be especially excited to work with HPD, applicants, and neighborhood stakeholders to stand up the BSA Fast Track for affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: This is an action with the potential to bring affordable housing to every part of the city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: With this action, BSA can play a bigger role in our collective ongoing efforts to build a fairer, more inclusive city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you again for offering the opportunity to testify, and I'm happy to answer any questions that you might have.

chapters.summary: Ung notes the Council has no formal role in BSA decisions and asks how Mangin would weigh council member input. Mangin commits to a completely open door policy, taking council input into careful consideration within BSA's legal constraints.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Mangin on council input in BSA proceedings

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So we're just going to start with my questions, then the committee members'questions, and then we'll go to other members.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So first, members of the council can wait in a BSA proceeding just like any other person can.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: But we also know that the council does not have any decision-making powers over the matters that go before BSA, correct?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: No direct decision-making powers, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So what is your view of the way that should be given a court to any input for a local council member about BSA project that is in their local community in relation to whether a BSA should approve a project?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, at BSA, I would have a completely open door policy with respect to any input from council members on projects that affect their district.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Community board review is built in to virtually every BSA action as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And while, as we discussed,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: BSA actions are typically very legally constrained.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, if you meet the findings, it gets approved.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: If you don't meet the findings, you may not approve it.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Within that tightly cabined discretion, I would promise to take into careful consideration the input of any council members on those actions.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Mangin states the Council should play a central role in planning and land use as established by the 1989 charter. He believes local voices are paramount but aren't the only voices that matter for decisions with broader community or citywide effects.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Mangin on council's role in shaping land use outcomes

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And what role do you believe the council members should play in shaping land use outcomes?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And where should the balance?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Council Doherty lied between local elected officials who are on the ground in the community and expert agencies.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I firmly believe that city council plays, should play a central role in planning and land use decisions in New York City.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That is where they were placed by the 1989 charter, which guides decision making to this day.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I believe that local voices are paramount when it comes to projects, but also, you know, a big theme of my career is that local voices aren't the only voices that matter for land use decisions that have

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: an effect on a broader community or even citywide.

chapters.summary: Ung presses for specifics on how Mangin will take council views seriously. Mangin commits to an open door policy and to addressing council member input in the decision record, noting whether the board acted on or acknowledged the input.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Mangin on commitment to address council concerns in decisions

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So what commitments can you make to this body that will assure us that you, in fact, take the views and concerns about any given project before the BSA seriously, and not just dismiss it, because the council has no formal role in the process?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You have my commitment that I would take those views into consideration, again, within the legal strictures that guide BSA actions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I would also point to my record.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think that probably the biggest theme

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: of my career, as I mentioned in my opening statement, has been to support fair outcomes by ensuring that all people have a voice in the land use.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: decisions that affect them.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And that very much includes the paramount local voices.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So thank you for making that commitment today.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Can you give us a little bit more detail what that commitment entails?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Well, I would certainly commit again to having an open door policy with any comments that local council members had on individual applications and beyond that commit to addressing that input in any

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: decision record of the body, noting

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: in a straightforward way, the input provided by council member and also the board's response to that input, whether it was to take it and in some way modify the approval in response to it,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: or whether it was to acknowledge it, not act on it.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Or so forth and so forth, but to report it in the decision record.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So you're saying the council members'concerns will be addressed, whether or not it's, you know, you're going to agree with it or not agree with it, it will be addressed in the final decision?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Ung asks about CBAs and when trade-offs are justified. Mangin calls CBAs a useful tool, citing $5 billion in City of Yes and $413 million in Jamaica, but cautions that CBAs shouldn't be so costly they prevent projects from happening. He declines to give a specific example of when they're not justified.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Mangin on community benefits agreements and trade-offs

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: You have stated that the community benefits agreement involves trade-offs.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Can you please expand on those trade-offs and in view of your view, when are those trade-offs justified and when they are not?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, community benefits agreements, I firmly believe.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: that they are a very useful tool to get projects to yes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I want to get that out of the open.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The trade-offs that I've referred to in the past are at times, when crafting community benefits agreements, we all have to be careful.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That we are enabling feasibility for that project and that the community benefits agreements aren't, for instance, so costly that it prevents projects from happening.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think that we've all seen instances of this in New York City.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Happily, we've also seen instances, large and small,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: of approvals, you know, like City of Yes for Housing Opportunity at the biggest end, $5 billion of community benefits in order to support that new housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, $413 million as part of the Jamaican neighborhood rezoning.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Or even smaller scales, individual projects in districts that have open space constraints that are underserved by open space, where new projects get approved along with new publicly accessible open space in order to support that housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Those are all huge win-win situations that help to

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: demonstrate how these approvals benefit not just the people who move into the housing, but also the broader community.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And again, I think community benefits agreements are an incredibly useful tool to get there.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So when are they not justified?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's not a matter, thank you for the question, it's not a matter of justified or not justified.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's just maintaining consciousness of making sure that projects remain feasible and that the community benefits are not so costly that it prevents the project itself and those community benefits from coming to fruition.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of that, just in the past?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think I'd want to get back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: To do a little more research on that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay, sure.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Community benefits grievance also often negotiate to address local concerns about development.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: What role, if any, do you believe the agreement should play in ensuring that communities share in the benefits of the new development?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think that they can play an incredibly important role in a range of applications.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We mentioned at the highest end, the $5 billion intended to support the additional 80,000 units created by, enabled by City of Yes for Housing Opportunity.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, the $400 million of improvements to, for instance, the sewer systems in Jamaica in order to make those work.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And then, you know, through environmental review, identifying when projects may have impacts, for instance, on school seats.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Publicly accessible open space, on transportation, and then ensuring that those projects come along with, you know, the new entrance to the subway necessary for that project to make planning sense,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: or the additional publicly accessible open space necessary in order for that project to have a land use rationale, or the millions of dollars in payments to create new school seats to support the children that will be brought to the neighborhood for those projects.

chapters.summary: Ung contrasts DCP's user-friendly ZAP portal with BSA's limited website. Mangin commits to prioritizing website improvements to function more like ZAP, and to posting all applications, materials, environmental review documents, and public submissions online.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Mangin on BSA website transparency commitments

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Moving on to a separate topic.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the DCP's public accessible website known as the Zoning Application Portal, known as ZAP?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I am, yes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And will you agree that ZAP is a website that's user-friendly and well-organized and make it easy to find information, including all the application materials?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I would agree, Chair, I would agree that it's much better than the public interface that existed before.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So are you familiar with the BSA's website?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So, I think you know where I'm going with this.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We often hear from our constituents and staff that the BSA website lacks basic transparency and is very limited in the information it provides, which makes it difficult for the public and for us to know and understand what the board is considering when decisions are being made.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: When you commit to this council that you become chair, you will prioritize improving the transparency and information that's available on the BSA website, such that it functions more like the ZAP portal.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But you've sort of scooped me here.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I wanted the opportunity to announce that something like that is high up on the list of things that I would like to do.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: If confirmed, I think that reaches back to some of the earliest...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: My earliest work experience right after law school where we were trying to create publicly accessible, legible, more accessible

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: tools so that people could understand what's going on in order to participate if and when they wanted to, you know, all the way up through

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: my experience at DCP where I've observed and participated in these efforts that I think could be beneficial at the BSA as well.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So would you then commit?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: to posting all applications, materials, environmental review documents, and public submissions online.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, Chair, I would commit to that.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Ung asks whether the Council has legal authority to require BSA transparency improvements and whether it's fair to disregard community concerns. Mangin commits to the improvements without needing legislation and says local voices are paramount even if not always decisive.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Mangin on council legal authority and disregarding local concerns

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Do you believe, and since you're committing to it, but if somehow it doesn't happen, do you believe the council has legal authority to require the BSA to do that?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm not totally sure.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I don't want to be answering legal questions that may implicate charter issues on the fly.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I commit to doing it.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I'd have to get back to you on any of the legal questions.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Let's hope we don't have to come down to that.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: But thank you for the commitment.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: With your understanding that you can't please everyone, would you agree it's fair, it isn't fair, to disregard the concerns of the affected communities as they perceive the impacts of new development coming into their neighborhood,

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: particularly with BSA approvals, because that would invariably mean that development would not be complying with existing zoning rules.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, I mean, I believe that local voices are paramount when it comes to land use decisions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That doesn't mean that they're always decisive, but I do hold them as paramount.

chapters.summary: Mangin describes his approach of meeting with anyone who wants to discuss applications. On engagement metrics, he focuses on making the public interface accessible, training community groups about BSA processes, and ensuring participation infrastructure exists before controversial applications arise.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Mangin on philosophy for local concerns and engagement metrics

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Can you describe your philosophy for giving meaningful consideration to local concerns while balancing the legal standards governing variances, special permits, and appeals to the board has the power to grant?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, throughout my career, I've been happy to meet and discuss individual applications or broader policy issues with anybody who would like to meet and discuss those issues.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I would carry that through if I'm at BSA.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: As we've discussed, BSA actions are very legally constrained.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Within that, though, I commit to acknowledging, describing, and responding to any feedback that comes from a member of the public all the way up to members of the city council.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And what metrics will you use to determine whether BSA is successfully engaging with the communities?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm not sure what metrics would be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I do think that, as we discussed, we can make the public interface at BSA more accessible, more legible than it is today.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We can't force people to interact with it.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But I believe first off that if people do want to interact with it as part of an individual application, that should be as easy as possible.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And as I was discussing with Councilmember Epstein earlier as well, wanting to train community groups about what the BSA does, how it works, and how to participate.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So that before an individual application comes around that might be controversial or might get a lot of attention, that system is in place for those groups or those individuals to participate.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And again, that goes back to some of my earliest experience in land use in New York City, and I think it carries through nicely to this role.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Will you support publishing annual reports showing how the community board recommendations compared to the final BSA decisions?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I certainly can look into it.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, at Housing Division at City Planning, my team,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: does a fair amount of annual reporting requirements and we do

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: you want to balance those types of reporting requirements with the pipeline of existing work to do.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It sounds like something to explore, but I don't think I can commit to it at this time.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Ung asks about monitoring enforcement of BSA conditions and publishing annual reports comparing community board recommendations to final decisions. Mangin says approvals are recorded against properties but he needs to learn more about enforcement. He declines to commit to annual reports at this time.
chapters.title: Chair Ung Q&A: Mangin on enforcement of BSA conditions and annual reports

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And how will you ensure that conditions imposed on BSA variances and special permits are actually monitored and enforced after approval?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, those approvals, I believe, are recorded against the property so that they are available for all to understand and to be enforced going forward.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: As far as the existing system of enforcement, I'm...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
