utterances.text: I have some learning to do on how that exactly works over time, but obviously enforcement is crucial to any kind of decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Now I'd like to pass it off to our Deputy Speaker, Williams.

chapters.summary: Williams thanks Mangin for Jamaica Neighborhood Plan work and confirms his role as policy director for the 2025 Charter Revision Commission, noting the council felt some proposals were hostile to their powers. Mangin acknowledges his involvement.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams Q&A: Mangin on Jamaica plan and charter revision role

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Hi, John.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Hello, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you so much for all of your work on the Jamaican Neighborhood Plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I really appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know I worked really closely with the former DCP chair, because I do believe every district needs to play a role in producing housing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I just want to say that my concern really isn't on the macro level of housing supply, but really how we understand neighborhood level.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: issues, whether it be gentrification or displacement, particularly in historically black homeowner communities like Southeast Queens.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So a lot of my questions, I know when we met, you kind of explained a lot of the other things with your writing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So most of my questions will actually focus on your written responses to the council.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So the first thing I did want to say in terms of your former role as director of policy and research with the 2025 Charter Revision Commission, it is fair to say that

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: you were involved in drafting, if not the actual language, but at least the concepts of the findings and requirements for the new

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: fast track BSA zoning, and I'd say quite a few other hostile, I think us in the council, we feel like some of them were a little hostile to us and how we see our powers.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Is that

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: a correct statement that you were a part of that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I just want to make sure we're on the same page.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for the question, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I was the policy director for the 2025 Charter Revision Commission that largely involved

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: trying to examine, shape the sort of the fire hose of proposals that were coming from members of the public, from Charter Revision Commissioners, and others.

chapters.summary: Williams asks how Mangin reconciles praising the council's housing role with participating in stripping council land use powers. Mangin argues the charter changes maintained the council's central role with minor adjustments for affordable housing types ULURP was bad at handling.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams Q&A: Mangin on reconciling council role with charter changes

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, and then in your opening statement, which, thank you, you did note that the council was instrumental and is instrumental in helping to build housing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But for me, and, you know, I know...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: quite a few of my other colleagues that were here last year during the Charter Review Commission felt like

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: our commitment to building housing wasn't really appreciated and or received because many of the proposals that we had tried to

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: get amended in the final questions, none of them were actually taken up.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So how do you sort of reconcile, you know, your openness statement that the council is so instrumental and important in housing, but then also on the back end, sort of be a part of an effort to strip away.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Council powers as it pertains to land use matters.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Council has and should have a central role in land use decisions, land use and planning decisions in the city, and they, of course, still do.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: If I could provide some perspective on what the Charter Revision Commissioners were trying to do, in my view, and what the voters approved, it was essentially to maintain

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: the Council's role as it has existed since 1989 with a few

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: relatively minor adjustments to address types of applications or types of housing that ULERP was demonstrably bad at, given the three or four decades.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: of experience with it.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And that included relatively modest increases in zoning.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, one of the things that I did personally do on the Charter Vision Commission, I looked at the last 10 years of rezonings, and there were zero rezonings for 30% or less increase in housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And, you know, as we all know, many communities get concerned when there are big changes to zoning.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And these are types of changes that may not raise those same issues with communities while also enabling, you know, for growth and change over time.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So I think the commissioners saw that as an issue.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Like, you can't do small changes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You've got to do big things that create anxieties.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Or, you know, parts of the city that saw virtually zero affordable housing production over the last couple decades.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So ULERP was not good for that, was not working for that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So while maintaining council's role and ULERP as it has existed since 1989,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: making relatively minor adjustments to enable certain types of affordable housing or more modest actions that had not been possible since then.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So in my view, I believe that council absolutely retains its central role in housing and planning and land use.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In the city with a couple minor adjustments in order to make projects happen that could not happen under the previous system.

chapters.summary: Williams challenges Mangin's claim that housing scarcity in affluent neighborhoods drives gentrification. Mangin argues the 1.4% vacancy rate fundamentally drives high costs, displacement, and segregation, and that decisions not to build in wealthier areas create pressure on lower-income neighborhoods.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams Q&A: Mangin on gentrification and displacement causes

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, and I did appreciate some of your answers where you mentioned some of the proposals you had suggested to the commission that weren't actually achieved to address some of the

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: issues that you referenced and also the historical context that you provided around like term limits.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And, you know, it's true, like we kind of come and go after eight years with.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Term limits.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So it's a different type of crop of members.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I did appreciate your thoughtful questions there.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So this is the next questions are really about your responses.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So the city's own displacement methodology treats displacement as the interaction of vulnerability, housing conditions, and market pressure.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So in your written responses, you say that gentrification and displacement in many lower income communities of color have been driven by land use decisions in wealthier neighborhoods, and you describe housing shortages in exclusionary areas as a root cause.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Are you saying that restricted supply in affluent neighborhoods is the primary cause of gentrification in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: One significant cause among several or simply one contributor to broader housing market pressures?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think that among members of council, among administrations, among many of the groups that work on

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: housing in New York City.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: There's just a greater understanding and acknowledgement that the housing shortage,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: you know, this 1.4% vacancy rate that we're dealing with, is what drives, on a fundamental level, high housing costs, gentrification and displacement pressures, overcrowding, homelessness, segregation, and everything else.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so if you zero in on individual parts of the city that are experiencing significant gentrification and displacement pressures, like parts of central Brooklyn or East Brooklyn or, you know, northern Manhattan or the South Bronx,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I do think those are problems that are created by decisions that were made elsewhere, by decisions not to build in parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Contributing to that housing shortage, which thereby contributes to the gentrification and displacement pressures that the neighborhoods that I mentioned experience.

chapters.summary: Williams presses for empirical evidence. Mangin acknowledges housing scarcity isn't the only cause but calls it the root cause, citing the displacement risk index showing paycheck-to-paycheck families are most vulnerable. He notes a growing body of research over 25 years supports this view.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams Q&A: Mangin on empirical evidence for housing scarcity theory

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Do you have any empirical evidence of that?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because I know we had a very lengthy conversation, but when I hear words like driven by root cause, I'm like, well, what empirical evidence do we have that says it is only housing scarcity that is creating these issues?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Do you have any empirical evidence or things that you can direct me to to further understand?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: That theory and that stance you have.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's not the only cause, to be sure, but it's the fundamental root cause that we see.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Of course, when we're talking about

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: gentrification and displacement, we're also talking about lots of individual stories.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, the displacement risk index that you mentioned notes that the biggest factor in displacement, the biggest vulnerability factor is, you know, families who might be a paycheck or two away from not being able to pay the rent.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so when they experience a shock, you know, maybe there's a layoff or a health event or something like that and the income drops, those are the families that, you know, then

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: get hit the hardest by the housing shortage leading to difficulties for those families.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So it's not the only cause.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I would think of it as the root cause.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I would say that there is a growing body of research over the last 25 years or so that supports that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And there is increasingly good research on a sort of a smaller scale level that may make that realer for folks who can't quite see the macro picture.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, I know a lot of the studies that I saw speak to that, but then there are a ton of other studies that have so many other causal claims for, you know, displacement and gentrification.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I just wanted to know if you were pulling from specific studies.

chapters.summary: Williams cites research showing upzonings are associated with census tracts becoming whiter. Mangin acknowledges the study and argues broad-based approaches like City of Yes that ask all neighborhoods to contribute can address these concerns, and says he would not characterize Southeast Queens as wealthy exclusionary.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams Q&A: Mangin on upzoning research and Southeast Queens homeowners

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So New York City specific research has found that upzoning activity was positively and significantly associated with the odds of a census tract becoming whiter.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: thing that neighborhood upzonings can accelerate gentrification pressure in the short term.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Are you familiar with that research?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm not sure which particular study that you're referring to, but I'm happy to look at it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, it's by Jenna Davis, How Do Upzonings Impact Neighborhood Demographic Change?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It's in the Land Use Policy Academic Journal.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So given the strength of your statements about the causes of gentrification, shouldn't evidence pointing in the opposite neighborhood level direction be a part of your analysis?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And when you mentioned the author of that piece,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I have seen that a couple years back.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's a few years old.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I would say this is one of the reasons why at City Planning,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: have always advocated for broad-based approaches to addressing the housing shortage that drives gentrification and displacement.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And neighborhood studies that pay attention to parts of the city that may not have been pulling their fair share in terms of housing production.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So like the Soho-Noho neighborhood rezoning, for instance.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And if we're taking a broad-based approach to creating housing,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And if we're paying special attention to maybe some of the wealthier, whiter parts of the city that have not contributed to housing,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: production, then we can address some of those issues that are raised by that study.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I fully understand, sympathize, agree with communities, maybe lower income communities of colors who say, why us?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And that is one of the big reasons why

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, we focused on City of Yes for Housing Opportunity that asks all neighborhoods to contribute.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, just a few more questions specifically around homeowners.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know, you know, obviously in your responses, you repeatedly contrast lower income communities of color with wealthier neighborhoods that use political power to restrict housing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But that binary does not describe large parts of Southeast Queens, as you know, you and I discussed, you know, largely black and brown homeowners that are working in middle class.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Would you characterize the Southeast Queens community as the kind of wealthy exclusionary community your theory is directed at?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: No, I would not, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I'm a huge supporter of homeownership in general.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I recognize the opportunities that it creates for stability, for wealth creation across generations, and I'm in no way opposed to homeownership.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mentioned my...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: My last job before I came to city planning was to create limited equity co-ops in partnership with black and Latino tenant associations in DC so that they could access

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: the benefits of home ownership.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's City of Yes for Housing Opportunity.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Personally eliminated the obstacles in the zoning to affordable homeownership projects.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And it's just part of the broader sweep of the fair housing work that I've engaged in over the course of my career.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Housing choice is not just about neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's also choice about what type of housing that you want to live in.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: For some families, it's going to be an apartment in a central location.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: For others, it's going to be a one or two family.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Home a little farther out in the city, and our housing policies should support that full range of choices.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

chapters.summary: Williams asks what framework should apply when historically black working-class homeowner communities raise development concerns. Mangin cites the Jamaica plan's balance of higher densities in appropriate areas, sewer infrastructure investments, and protecting low-density districts. Williams notes she had to fight for the sewer funding.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams Q&A: Mangin on framework for black homeowner community concerns

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: All of that said, what framework do you think should apply then when residents of historically black working and middle class homeowner communities raise concerns about development?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: As you noted in your written response, as you noted today, you know, you were a part of the Jamaican neighborhood plan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You weren't necessarily on the grounds fielding the complaints, but it was very difficult.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The community board, both community boards actually voted it down and I still worked with the previous

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Administration to push that through despite a lot of local political challenges.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I think for me, I try to strike a balance in understanding what those concerns are.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so just wanted to know, you know, your thoughts on what type of framework should be considered for these communities that maybe on the face might feel like you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But as you so eloquently stated, you're not.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So what framework would you apply to those communities who do have some concerns about development in their communities?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, I've been to Community Board 12.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Many times and I understand those concerns and they absolutely have to be considered, have to be listened to, have to be taken into account.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I think that the Jamaica Neighborhood Plan

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: struck that balance in an extremely effective way, including higher densities in parts of the neighborhood that were appropriate, and higher densities in one part of the neighborhood can take some of the pressure off of some of the lower density parts of the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think that using the Jamaica Neighborhood Plan to leverage hundreds of millions of dollars for improvements to the sewer infrastructure

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: was a fantastic win as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And it's why, you know, when considering...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, that I had to fight for.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The administration did not want to do it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I just want to add that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: They did not want to do it.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It was a fight.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I, it was, it was a legendary, legendary fight, yes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And, you know, over the course of my time at City Planning, have advocated for policies that don't put a target

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: on those low-density neighborhoods, but rather take a broader perspective, acknowledging that if we all contribute, that we can address the housing shortage, the policy problems that are...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: from the housing shortage without having significant impacts on sensitive areas, neighborhood character and sensitive areas like one and two family districts in Southeast Queens.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, I'll just ask one more question.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know my colleagues have questions.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So for generations, black families were excluded from neighborhoods and conventional mortgage credit through redlining, steering, discriminatory lending, and other barriers.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Southeast Queens became one of the places where black families built home ownership and intergenerational wealth despite those barriers.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Do you recognize a meaningful distinction between affluent communities using zoning to keep people out and historically excluded black homeowners using the democratic process to protect their ability to stay?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, the second, I've taught land use law at NYU for maybe nine years now, and the second class every year, we read Richard Rothstein, The Color of Law, Ta-Nehisi Coates,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: case for reparations, the chapter of Kenneth Jackson's Crabgrass Frontier that addresses exactly those issues that you're discussing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So it's something that I feel I understand, that I try to convey to others.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's always one of the...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Most engaged classes that I have with my students.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so I absolutely understand that distinction.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'll just come back for the second round.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you, Deputy Speaker.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Now I'd like to pass it on to Council Member Banks.

chapters.summary: Banks questions whether Mangin still stands by his article arguing housing advocates should embrace development of all types. Mangin confirms he still believes housing shortages drive a range of problems and that building more of all types is necessary.
chapters.title: CM Banks Q&A: Mangin on 2014 article advocating housing of all types

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, and good to see you again, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Madgen.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for coming to my district yesterday and having a meaningful conversation.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Madgen, first of all, I would like to begin with some of your past writings, because I believe they provide important insight into your views on housing and land use matters.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know, as the council considers your nomination, I want to better understand who the real John Madgen is

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: and what philosophy, perspective, and judgment you would bring to the Board of Standards and Appeals should you be confirmed.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know, in 2014, writing by you titled The New Exclusionary Zoning, you argued that the housing advocacy community should move away from

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: what you described as, quote, reflectivity anti-development sentiments.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And embrace increased housing development, quote, of all types.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Do you still stand by that position today?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And looking back, how has your thinking evolved regarding the relationship

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: between new development, affordability, and displacement.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: As I mentioned in my opening statement, first off, I should say that absolutely we need to address the housing shortage.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We need to build more housing of all types in order to address those range of policy problems that

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: you know, people in neighborhoods like yours experience, whether it's high housing costs, gentrification and displacement pressure, you know, homelessness, overcrowding, segregation, you know, a housing market where tenants have no power.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: All of those things emerge from the housing shortage.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So I absolutely still believe that we need to build housing of all types in order to address that range of problems for real New Yorkers.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about the role of local communities in shaping what gets built. Mangin reiterates local voices are paramount but not the only voices, and that problems in individual communities can't be solved entirely by that community alone.
chapters.title: CM Banks Q&A: Mangin on local community role in shaping development

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And what role do you believe local communities should have in shaping what gets built in their neighborhoods?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how would you view or inform your decision making at the BSA?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Local voices are paramount in the process, in the land use process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: They're not the only voices, but I think they're paramount.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And, you know, when we went on the walking tour yesterday and saw

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: housing that was created by East Brooklyn

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: congregations and others and some of the gateway project.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, it's just an amazing testament to what local communities can do, what they can build in collaboration with, you know, citywide officials.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Also in mind then, though, is that, you know,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The problems that communities like yours face can't be solved entirely by that community itself.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It also needs action on a more citywide level.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so just making sure that your community has a voice in the full range of decisions that have affected

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: it over the decades.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So local voices are paramount.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: They're not the only voices that matter.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so wanting to ensure that all affected voices are included.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for that response.

chapters.summary: Banks quotes Mangin's article calling downzoning, CBAs, rent control, and affordable housing focus 'kludgy,' defined as awkward and poorly designed. Mangin clarifies all those tools are useful and essential, and his only point was that advocates should also push for more housing supply alongside those tools.
chapters.title: CM Banks Q&A: Mangin on 'kludgy' characterization of housing advocacy tools

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: In the same article, you characterize down zoning, community benefit agreements, the lengthy approval processes,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: rent control, and even a focus on affordable housing over other forms of development as a part of what you call kludgy, K-L-U-D-G-Y,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: approach by housing advocacy community.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And when I looked up the definition of kludgy, I wanted to, it says kludgy is an informal adjective that describes something.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: awkward, poorly designed, clumsy, or patched together as a temporary fix.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: That's, I would say, that's a broad collection of policies and protections that tenants, housing advocates, and communities and elected officials have relied upon.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What did you believe the housing advocacy community was getting wrong, and which of these views do you still hold today?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thanks for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So I believe that all of those things you mentioned are useful tools, some of them absolutely essential.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Things like community benefits agreements, rent stabilization, absolutely essential.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: My only point there.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Was that we also need to be doing this other thing along with those things, which is ensuring that we are building enough housing to address increasing housing shortages.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The paper was not about New York City.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It was about cities across the country, an increasing number of which we're experiencing, are experiencing housing shortage that drive this range of policy issues that we deal with every day.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So while all those things you mentioned, CBAs, rent stabilization, et cetera, are extremely important, have their uses, my argument was that we, the housing advocacy community, also have to advocate for more housing of all types to address the housing shortage.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what 'all types' means in a low-income community facing displacement. Mangin says it means multifamily, affordable at a range of incomes, one-to-two family homes, and market rate housing to accommodate demand that otherwise pressures lower-income neighborhoods.
chapters.title: CM Banks Q&A: Mangin on housing of all types in low-income displacement communities

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Also, you argued for housing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: development, housing development of all types.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What does housing development of all types mean to you today in a low-income community facing displacement pressures?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What role should a market rate or luxury development play?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how do you ensure that the people already living there will actually benefit?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: When I say housing of all types, you know, I generally mean all types, multifamily, affordable, at a range of incomes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: One and two family homes can be appropriate in different parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Market rate housing, also incredibly important to, you know, accommodate some of that demand, which is ultimately what puts pressure on lower income neighborhoods across the city when people with money

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: go looking for housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In a city that doesn't have enough of it, they are going to start to put pressure on the central Brooklyn and northern Manhattan and the South Bronx and parts of Queens.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So all types means all types.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Families in New York City have an extreme diverse range of needs and wants.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And ideally,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: we can create a housing policy that accommodates all of them.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I just want to continue to walk you through.

chapters.summary: Banks questions Mangin's comparison of community meeting participants to Tea Party activists. Mangin explains he was referencing jurisdictions with open meetings laws that would outlaw private conversations between council members and applicants, which would prevent negotiating CBAs. He wasn't talking about New York specifically.
chapters.title: CM Banks Q&A: Mangin on Tea Party comparison and NIMBY participation

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: some of your past writings and see how they conflict with some of the things that you're now subscribing to today.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it comes to community participation and this Tea Party comparison,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: In that same article, while discussing public participation and open government requirements, you ask readers to imagine

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Tea Party activists being present during a high-level federal budget negotiations.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Using that analogy in discussing NIMBY participation at planning board meetings or community board meetings, as we know it now, what exactly

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: were you trying to communicate with that comparison, and do you still stand by that today?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Going back to the earliest days of my career, I am a huge supporter of community participation in planning decisions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think my record demonstrates that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Did you realize, does Councilmember, some other jurisdictions have laws that would outlaw conversations between individual council members and applicants in the land use process?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That means you would not be able to talk to them at all.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You wouldn't be able to talk to a developer during the process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That would make it very difficult for individual council members

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: to hammer out those types of community benefits agreements that we've been talking about that are so important to making communities understand the value of individual projects.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So in that part, I was just saying that we should not have laws, such as exist in some other jurisdictions, that outlaw council members talking to applicants

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's a routine thing that happens today in New York on the way towards meaningful community benefits agreements.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But with the comparison to the Tea Party?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The idea is you would not be able to have any private discussions without extreme proponents or extreme opponents in the room with you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That would make it really hard to hammer out those negotiations to get to yes on projects.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so just advocating for a process much like exists in New York City where you can have those conversations, you can negotiate benefits for the community.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So I wasn't talking about New York.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In that particular passage.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how Mangin determines whether opposition is legitimate. Mangin says he never thinks of input as legitimate or illegitimate. Banks then asks him to reconcile his writings about NIMBYs with saying communities should be heard; Mangin points to his career-long support for broad participation.
chapters.title: CM Banks Q&A: Mangin on legitimate opposition and reconciling writings with current views

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, let's imagine for a moment that residents from the 42nd Council District opposed the development

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: because of concerns about displacement, infrastructure, lack of parking, affordability, or even changes to the neighborhood's character.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How would you determine whether those residents are legitimately protecting their community or simply standing in the way of development?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And where do you draw the line?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, local voices are absolutely paramount.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I don't, I never think of it in terms of, is this input legitimate?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Is this not legitimate?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's all input, and when it comes from the local community, it deserves a central place in the consideration of those actions.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: In your responses to the council, you say neighborhood input should be listened to, quote, most closely and carefully, unquote,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: while also saying neighborhood voices should not be unilaterally decisive.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Help me reconcile that with your earlier writings about NIMBYs and anti-development activists and public processes that can delay housing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When you say communities should be held, heard, what does that actually mean in practice?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, I truly believe that the voices of everyone affected by land use decisions should be part of the decision-making process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I don't think that's always been the case in New York City.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Like I outlined in my responses to council questions as well, I think some of the neighborhoods that we think of as being under extreme pressure

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In New York City.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, the central Brooklands, the east Brooklands, northern Manhattan, south Bronx, parts of Queens.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Those are a result of decisions that were made elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: My division, we made a map.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We looked at sort of all the different types of protective land use actions that were taken in New York City since the 1960s.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, down zonings or restrictive special districts or limited height districts or things like that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And when we created that map, you could see the neighborhoods that were under pressure today.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: They were the blank spaces on the map.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Those were the areas that were not protected.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And that, to me, illustrated in stark graphic terms the way decisions made in other parts of the city affected those blank spaces on the map.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so it's just, if you go back to the paper, if you go back to big city-wides like City of Yes for Housing Opportunity,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's all a piece of the same theme, the same argument, that everybody who is affected by a land use decision should have a voice in the process.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Madam Chair, I just have a couple more questions, if you may indulge.

chapters.summary: Banks asks for an example where community opposition would cause BSA to reject or change an application advancing housing goals. Mangin notes BSA's site-specific approvals provide more latitude than rezonings to accommodate local input within legal constraints.
chapters.title: CM Banks Q&A: Mangin on when community opposition would change BSA decisions

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Give me an example of circumstances where community opposition would cause BSA to reject or materially change an application.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: That otherwise advances the city's housing goals.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: One thing I like about BSA is that they're all site-specific applications.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: They're a particular project with a particular owner.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That contrasts with what DCP is typically doing, which is a, the City Planning Commission is typically doing, which is a rezoning.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: A rezoning allows what it allows.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The city planning commission and council often are limited in how they can respond to community comments.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: An R8A is an R8A.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You can't customize it in response to community comments.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: If the BSA, it's a site-specific, owner-specific approval.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That provides more latitude, again, within the legal constraints that the BSA operates, to accommodate local input, community input.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And that's something that I would absolutely look forward to doing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks at what point CBA demands impede development. Mangin says it's about maintaining feasibility, not reasonableness, and that actors with leverage should keep project viability in mind. Banks asks who makes that determination; Mangin says it emerges from a political process.
chapters.title: CM Banks Q&A: Mangin on CBAs and when demands become unreasonable

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I think you had addressed the, well, I guess I'll just ask this question anyway again about the CBA agreements, where you currently stand on community benefits agreements.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And do you believe that they are important tools to communities negotiating major development projects?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Or do you still view them as something that can impede housing production?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I know that question was kind of phrased to you earlier, but I want to, again, get you on the record as to, you know, comparing that to your past statements or your writings to where do you stand right now?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Then as now, I think CBAs are a useful tool and sometimes an extremely useful and wonderful tool

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: in order to underscore that some of these actions, like City of Yes for Housing Opportunity, like some of the neighborhood rezonings where there's a negotiated package of capital improvements, to underscore that those can be win-win, that it's not the city versus a neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It is the city working with neighborhoods in order to address citywide needs while at the same time providing the investments that communities need to thrive into the future.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And at what point does the community's demand for benefits become unreasonable?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Or impede, or it can be an impediment to development based off of your writing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's not a matter of reasonable or unreasonable so much as, again, just trying to keep an eye on feasibility.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I don't know, for instance, whether

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: This is a result of negotiated community benefits agreements, but can think of some projects over the years that, you know, the administration or council,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: negotiated for more affordable housing or payment for this or that that just haven't come to fruition and just trying to make sure that we are not

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: blocking the underlying housing and the benefits that are supposed to come along with it via community benefits agreements that don't that don't quite work as a policymaker it's just

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I feel like that's guidance that have to give to whether it's my superiors at city planning or in community board meetings or council, just have to keep an eye on that fundamental question of feasibility.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And who should make that determination?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The developer, the city, like the officials or the people who actually live there?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It emerges from a political process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I suppose that it's just an argument that the actors in that political process, the folks who have the leverage, whether it's the mayor, whether it's city council or whoever,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: should just keep that in mind when hammering out these community benefits agreements, just trying to make sure that we're creating something that works for everybody.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks questions Mangin's use of 'homeowner cartels' in his 2014 article. Mangin says it's a term of art from fair housing literature referring to municipalities where homeowners have decisive voice, not his coinage and not applicable to NYC. Banks presses on whether homeowners opposing density are characterized as cartels; Mangin says the term doesn't imply a particular policy orientation.
chapters.title: CM Banks Q&A: Mangin on 'homeowner cartels' terminology

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And my last question, and I'll come back in the second round.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I know you had mentioned in your writings you compared homeowners to cartels.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: In the first sentence of your article in the new exclusionary zoning, you referred to a homeowner.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: As cartels, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, I'm a huge supporter of homeownership opportunities.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I just want to answer that question.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Did you refer to homeowners as cartels?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's a term of art from the literature that is not mine.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's a descriptive term from fair housing literature.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But do you agree?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Based on the context when you wrote that article that homeowners are cartels.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I'll go even further.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Do you characterize homeowners who oppose additional density as cartels?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: No, certainly not all homeowners are parts of homeowner cartels.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's a term of specific meaning.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: That oppose density, homeowners that oppose density.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Homeowner cartels is a term of art from the fair housing literature that doesn't imply any particular orientation towards policy questions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's just, it's a term from the literature.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I didn't coin it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I just want to, for the record, the homeowners that participate in the same public process

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: that is available to all residents, right?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: This is a process that communities are involved in or able to engage in, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The land use review?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Yet, you described the participation as a cartel behavior, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't recall the passage that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you disagree with the position because you support allowing greater density in areas currently zoned for single-family homes?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I've lost the thread, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I guess I'll come back around to the line of questions.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I just wanted to kind of get clarification as to the term you had used.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It's called homeowners cartels.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And why was that term used to describe homeowners?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know, normal folks would take that offensively, especially when they're advocating for their community, and they want to make sure that

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: the character of the community is not changing and the folks that invested in their community, their views and input is being respected.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But thank you, Chair, for indulging and allowing me to get my questions through.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I'll come back in a second.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And I'm going to pass it on to Council Member Krishna.

chapters.summary: Krishnan discusses the false binary between supply-side and tenant protection approaches, arguing for holistic planning that addresses displacement, community infrastructure like schools and open space, and housing together. Mangin wholeheartedly agrees, citing his collaboration with tenant advocates and the evolution from concentrated to broad-based housing approaches.
chapters.title: CM Krishnan Q&A: Mangin on holistic planning and displacement lens

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Mangin.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's good to see you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Good to see you, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I appreciated our good conversation and get together a few weeks ago to talk about the issues.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And, you know, it's interesting, as we saw from our conversation, we sort of were on parallel tracks.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: While you were a lawyer in city planning, doing a lot of impressive work over the years, I was a lawyer representing communities in North Brooklyn and Western Queens hit hardest by displacement.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And, you know, my first case out of law school was the Broadway Triangle Fair Housing Litigation that lasted 10 years.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You wrote about that in your second Law Review article.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I read your Law Review articles.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You read mine.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We traded thoughts.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And it was interesting to see our perspectives during that time.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I think, you know, as we saw from our conversation, we both saw from our work in different spheres how urgent the housing crisis is today, how much we need to build and build quickly and build faster.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And, you know, one of the things that I wanted to do was just take a little bit of time to get there, but I do have a couple questions.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But before going to those questions, just to zoom out for a second, apart from your nomination, but the larger context that I think you and I have both seen over the years and where we are today,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: you know, we're in this urgent housing crisis, and at least what I've seen from my work.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And looking now at the public.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: discourse around housing, which I of course pay attention to in some spare time.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It seems to me like in the public discussion, like we've come to a sort of binary point in how we talk about housing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And kind of the views are put into two different boxes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: One is

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: being against development and anti-development, which I don't subscribe to and I reject.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And another one, which is how we need, because we are in such an urgent crisis, we have to build much more, we have to build faster, which is all absolutely true, but there's sometimes strands in the public discourse about how to do so.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We have to

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: limit or reduce community engagement because that can slow the process down and how we have to focus really exclusively on the number of units we build and supply as the way out of the crisis.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I believe absolutely we have to build more and we have to build quickly and cut out all of that

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: red tape where we can.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But my own experience has shown me that things I think are more nuanced about how we address the housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: That community voices, like in Broadway Triangle, can strengthen development and make sure they comply with fair housing laws, for example.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But that, you know,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There's a missing perspective that from my work, I think, is different from the binary that I see in public discussion today, which is,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: that we need to focus more on displacement as we think about the housing crisis, that as we build more and build new, we have to make sure we keep people in their homes and keep people in their communities that they've lived in for generations.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I've spent far too much time in tenants'kitchens and in their lobbies with buildings crumbling around them because landlords are destroying them to get them out of their homes, and especially that's the case in Williamsburg, Greenpoint, and Bushwick.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And to me, it seems like we have to build quickly and build fast, but also do so from a lens of displacement.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And when you think about it from a displacement standpoint, I think there are two ways in which community voices can combat displacement.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: One is because we can make sure when we develop and we build that

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: the housing is affordable to the neighborhoods that it's in.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And two, I think it helps us to think about housing in a more holistic way, where we're thinking about building new housing, but also about the services that should accompany that new housing build.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You take Jackson Heights, for example.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We're very dense, but our schools have been overcrowded for a very long time.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We have the least amount of green space in all of New York City.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: We and many communities have a major child care need, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so when we think about housing, we think about, well, how do we build and also the services to support that housing?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: More schools, more open space and green space.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: more better transit infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There's so much community infrastructure that I think should be folded into a more holistic and comprehensive view of how we think about building housing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I think that perspective, at least for me, has been missing from a lot of the public dialogue, and it comes from my own work.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I suspect you also agree with that, too, from what you've seen in your work over the years, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so my first question is, you know, given how...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Given our work over the years and what we've seen and how the housing crisis has been exacerbated over time,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I outlined all of this in the op-ed that I wrote very recently that I think you read too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But given where the housing crisis is, I think that our views have been shaped by all that's been happening over time, and we have to address all of these things together.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm curious, you know, in how you see your potential role as the head of leading BSA, how do you think, or even outside of BSA really, just in general, how do you see...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: The importance of holistic planning today, where we think about housing and also all the services that support the housing that come in.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How do you think about housing and community infrastructure together as we develop and as a solution to the housing crisis?

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks how Mangin would incorporate holistic planning values into BSA's separate process for variances that sidestep ULURP. Mangin describes BSA as a humbler but crucial role for individual projects, bringing his values to agenda-setting and individual applications within legal constraints.
chapters.title: CM Krishnan Q&A: Mangin on BSA's role in holistic planning for variances

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you very much for those questions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I want to wholeheartedly agree that I see that false binary out there as well, that pits supply folks.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: against tenant protection folks when, you know, I remember meeting with Dina Levy for Beers at China Chalet, you know, almost 10 years ago, talking about how these two things go together.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Right, exactly.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I've talked to her about that, too.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, Dina coming from the tenant protection side, me coming from the, you know, more from the supply side, and just seeing why are people...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Setting these up in opposition when they are so obviously complementary.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Exactly right.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That, of course, you need to have tenant-specific measures to prevent displacement.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: This urgent issue that's happening today, while at the same time you work to address those longer-term underlying conditions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, a colleague of mine, who I think has also been a colleague of Councilmember Epstein's at Urban Justice Center, had a tweet that one time hit me like a lightning bolt, which was, there are no tenants'rights at 1.4% vacancy.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Now, that's an exaggeration.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Of course, there are tenants'rights.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We have to fight for them as hard as we can, regardless of what the broader situation is.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But it just makes it so much harder to do the type of work that you are doing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Under conditions of extreme housing shortage as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So there's that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: There's that false binary.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And then there you asked about housing plus a broader view of what it takes in a community to make that housing appropriate from a land use perspective.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And you saw one poll, you know, Greenpoint, Williamsburg, you saw a neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It was a strategy where let's put.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: as much housing as we can in one place that has pretty significant consequences for a neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And it has costs for individual folks who may have been there before.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It wasn't just an underutilized manufacturing zone.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It was also a place where people lived.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I've seen just tremendous evolution on that front and that set of concerns over the last 10 years where we've moved from, you know, just putting a ton of new housing in one part of the city to

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: a broader approach that looks to create a lot of housing, yes, but over a much broader geography so that we can respect things like neighborhood, that we hear from neighborhoods about concerns about neighborhood character and rapid change,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: so that we can monitor and ensure.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That the infrastructure in those places is ready for additional housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so that, you know, if infrastructure needs to be augmented, if neighborhoods need investment, that that can come along with those actions as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so I see City of Yes for Housing Opportunity almost as like the opposite pole.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Instead of a ton of housing in one place, a little bit of housing everywhere.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: With the infrastructure improvements in order to support that over time.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So I, you know, you worked in a time and in a place that definitely looms really large in, I think, policymakers'minds in New York City.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I think that we have learned from that.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I appreciate your perspective on that.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I also appreciate you flagging that it's a false binary.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I think, you know, that's a great way to put it, too, because I do feel that we as a city have to break out of that false binary.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: I'm so glad we're talking much more about housing now.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I think, you know, you and I, many others in the housing movement have been calling attention to these issues for so long.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But now we've reached the point where everyone agrees we have to address it.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I think that sometimes the conversation, not only in the city, but really nationally, in abundance conversations, while all great, can lead us towards this false binary.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I don't think that we can subscribe to that.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It's more complex and nuanced, and I think makes for better development to ultimately solve the crisis.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: So I appreciate your view there and your sharing that perspective, too.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so another question I have is, you know, how do you now, you know, were you to lead BSA as well, there's a class of decisions that will come to you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: You know, one example, right, you know, there are variances that will come in front of you, too, that

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: sort of sidestep the rezoning process, which can be lengthy, and no doubt I understand the sentiments of we have to make our processes more efficient and cut out a lot of the bureaucracy in there.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: But, you know, there's a lot of value in those processes, too, that we have to preserve as well for better development.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: If you have things that come in front of you at BSA, be it a variant decision,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: That doesn't go through those standard planning processes.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How do you think about incorporating this view that we share about planning holistically, about not getting caught in the false binary?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: How do you think about that in your role as BSA chair?

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: When you have decisions that come in front of you,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: It could be a straightforward variance application, but I do believe there are ways in there to think more creatively about how we bring in these larger values that we share.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And I'm just wondering if you've given thought to how BSA could do more of that, since it is a separate process from what normally happens through rezonings or the land use processes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, BSA does represent a dramatic shift away from big citywide planning initiatives towards a humbler but still crucial

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: role of making individual projects work for, yes, for the landowner, but also for the neighborhood and also in line with our values as a city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And while it's received much less attention, I think one of the true joys of my time at City Planning has been, you know, the person that you can call who can address your problem.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And that includes, you know, calls from City Hall.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It includes calls from individual homeowners in, you know, low-density neighborhoods and parts of New York.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That I am some

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: somebody you can call and I will do my best to talk to the folks I need to talk to in order to answer your question or try to address that problem.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And, you know, I see BSA as a wonderful opportunity to be the person who can actually provide assistance, can provide help directly in those instances rather than trying to convince other people to go along with it.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And yes, I bring my values to the table as BSA chair.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, in many applications, those won't necessarily come to bear.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, again, it's a very legally constrained entity.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: When others do, I'll...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Do my best to incorporate input from the community, from council members and others in order to reach a resolution that works for the applicant and for the community at large.

chapters.summary: Krishnan asks whether Mangin sees combating displacement, engaging communities, and planning holistically as central to his BSA leadership. Mangin confirms yes, pointing to the BSA Fast Track's potential for publicly sponsored affordable housing in underserved areas as a key opportunity.
chapters.title: CM Krishnan Q&A: Mangin on bringing displacement and engagement values to BSA leadership

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And you do see your role as in BSA

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: you know, the values that we're talking about today, which you subscribe to as well, combating displacement, engaging communities, planning holistically, you do see those values as

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: important and having a role, a central role in your leadership of BSA.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: In other words, BSA, I don't think, I don't feel it should be this way, but is a,

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: There's sometimes a view, I think it has been this way in the past, where BSA is sort of just a separate entity altogether from the larger vision we have around housing.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: And so it would be a marked...

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: positive shift forward to have leadership at BSA that also sees that BSA is not just an entity that stamps variances and reviews non-zoning or

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: extra zoning applications, but that it's led from a point of values of combating displacement, of engaging communities, of planning holistically.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Do you see, in your leadership of BSA, bringing those values into the leadership of the agency?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, you may see it less in the context of individual applications and see it more in terms of agenda setting.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: As I mentioned, very excited about the potential for the BSA fast track.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: To create the types of projects that are, you know, almost universally acknowledged to be good, publicly sponsored affordable housing projects in

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: parts of the city that may not have seen as many in recent decades.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
