utterances.text: And, you know, the BSA has the ability now to save those projects a lot of time and a lot of money that can be used to create more housing or lower AMIs or otherwise tailor projects for their communities.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think there's a lot of potential there.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Now I'm going to pass it on to Minority Leader Carr.

chapters.summary: Carr asks how Mangin squares calling local voices paramount with referencing the Tea Party as radical. Mangin says he didn't call the Tea Party radical and was merely referencing groups passionately engaged in issues. He confirms political affiliation has no bearing on BSA decisions.
chapters.title: Minority Leader Carr Q&A: Mangin on Tea Party reference and political bias

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Mangin, for being here today.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I want to begin by referring to something that came up in a recent back and forth here at the hearing.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: You talked about in your response to questions that community voices are paramount in these discussions about land use.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And in referring to questions you had back and forth with Councilmember Banks, you referenced the Tea Party as a radical group.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Some of us represent districts and neighborhoods chock full of folks with that kind of politics.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So my question is, how do you square those two things that you said in your testimony that

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Local voices are paramount, but certain people's politics are radical.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Do people only have a paramount voice when they conform to John Mangin's view of what are mainstream politics?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Leader Carr.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, I firmly believe that

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Anybody affected by a land use decision should have a voice in the process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I believe that the local voices are paramount in that process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I didn't refer to the Tea Party as a radical group.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That was, I think, in the questions that I got from council on that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: By referencing Tea Party, I just meant groups that are intensely engaged in issues.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: At the time, 2014, they were an example of

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: groups that were passionately and intensely involved in a given set of issues, that's all.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It was meant to reflect the passion and intensity without, you know, casting any particular aspersions on it.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So the politics or partisan identification that a community is thought to have, actual or perceived, has no bearing in your view on a decision of the BSA or any land use decision?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Absolutely, I agree with that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It has no bearing whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Carr asks if Mangin views CBAs as poison pills. Mangin denies questioning the earnestness of council members negotiating CBAs and calls them positive tools. Carr then challenges the City of Yes EIS finding no significant negative impacts despite infrastructure deficits; Mangin notes the EIS identified impacts and the $5 billion in negotiated investments addressed them.
chapters.title: Minority Leader Carr Q&A: Mangin on CBAs as poison pills and City of Yes environmental review

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Going back to community benefit agreements, I know we've talked about it a lot at this hearing.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: In one of the articles that was referenced, the new exclusionary zoning, you put forward this idea that there are efforts to prevent particular developments to often go hand in hand with a variety of proposals, and then you go on to include the exaction of community benefits agreements to any development that does occur,

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: which seems to suggest that you see the pursuit of CBAs as not a genuine goal of stakeholders, but rather an attempt to create a poison pill for a particular development.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Can you expand upon that and what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Oh, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I actually don't think that I meant it in that way, that you suggested.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so you talked about– I don't question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I would never question the earnestness of council members or members of the community trying to negotiate a broader set of community benefits around a particular application.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That was not my intention.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Because community benefits have been particularly important things for the council.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: to negotiate on behalf, including the addition of more affordable housing units in some projects.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So you'd agree that CBAs on the whole have been a positive thing?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Like I say in the paper, they have their uses, and I've personally been involved in some of the negotiations around, you know, City of Yes for Housing Opportunity, around individual neighborhood rezonings.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Even around individual projects that require mitigations under environmental review.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I put that in the same bucket as well, and I think it's good and basic planning.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: So when a council member comes to you with a matter that may come before the BSA for a project to be finessed in some detail that could be

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: beneficial to a neighbor who may be getting an impact that didn't exist before, those are the sorts of things that you think should be taken into consideration when the BSA makes its determination?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Leader.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Within, again, the legal boundaries that pertain to any particular application, something like that should definitely be considered, yes.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: You talked about environmental review just a second ago.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: You know, there was an environmental review that was done as part of the city of Yes,

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: and there was a determination that there would be no significant negative impacts, despite the fact that many neighborhoods already lack basic water and sewage and utility infrastructure, little access to public transportation, there's overcrowded schools, there's traffic, there's pollution, all sorts of other things, flooding.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Do you agree with the finding of the EIS that was done into those?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Under those zoning applications?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: For City of Yes for Housing Opportunity?

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It identified a range of impacts, that EIS.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And yet we were asked to certify that there was no negative declaration when we had those.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It identified impacts.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Identifying impacts for a project does not definitively mean it can't be approved.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And then, you know, I would point back to the negotiations that secured $5 billion of capital investment and other community benefits in conjunction with the new housing.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Those are all benefits that the administration of the day resisted.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Council drove a hard bargain.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, I'm grateful for that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And to your credit, the city is in your debt.

chapters.summary: Carr questions why the charter revision focused on the council's 50-day ULURP role when the full development process averages 3.4 years. Mangin says the charter efforts were part of a range of streamlining efforts including pre-certification processes at DCP.
chapters.title: Minority Leader Carr Q&A: Mangin on charter revision and development timeline

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: You know, you were being very modest earlier about the scope of the changes of the charter revisions that were accomplished by the last Charter Revision Commission.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: There's been a recent analysis by Rebney that it takes about 3.4 years for a single new residential building in the city.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: It's an average of more than four, I think, in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And given that the council's role in ULERP that has been removed was, you know, at most 50 days, why wasn't there more focus in the revision commission on

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: the rest of the process, which clearly takes much longer, rather than on the council's role, which is a very small space in time when you consider the entire development.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for that question, Leader.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I would say the charter efforts were part of a range of similar efforts to address those issues.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I can say at City Planning, for instance, that we've been engaged in a pretty deep effort to try to streamline pre-certification processes for certain applications because, as you point out, it's not...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Just council, it's not just environmental review, it's not just DOB,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: you know, these are all parts of a single process, all of which should be examined in order to make sure that they're serving the policy goals that we as a city are headed toward.

chapters.summary: Carr again presses on the cartel term; Mangin clarifies it refers to smaller municipalities, not NYC. Carr then asks about housing demand projections; Mangin cites the administration's estimate of 700,000 units needed over 10 years. Carr asks about mandating set-asides for existing residents; Mangin says he hasn't considered that question.
chapters.title: Minority Leader Carr Q&A: Mangin on homeowner cartel term and housing demand projections

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Earlier in your discussion with Councilmember Banks, there was this discussion of the use of the term cartel in relation to, I guess, some homeowners in your view.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Could you clarify again what homeowners in your view engage in cartel behavior or are cartels?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, it's a term of art from the literature, the fair housing literature.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It generally refers to municipalities, typically smaller municipalities, where homeowners do have that entirely decisive voice on all matters of land use.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, the paper was not about New York City.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It was part of a national conversation, and so it borrowed that term to participate in that conversation.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But it's not a term that I would say.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Applies cleanly to anything in New York City.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: But do you see how homeowners listening to this hearing or having read articles where this was referenced could hear that as that makes you an appointee who's simply looking to

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: discount their views when it comes to the public process, even when it doesn't conform with the drive for more housing, even though there may be plenty of perfectly legitimate reasons why a project as proposed isn't sufficient?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: No, thank you, Leader.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, I'd point to the fact that I have worked to support homeownership opportunities throughout my career, whether in D.C.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: With lower-income populations or as part of Chi-A.-Ossé to try to restart the HPD pipeline of homeownership affordable, or even through parts of Chi-A.-Ossé that were intended to support homeownership and homeowners, whether it's

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: missing middle three-, four-, five-story apartment buildings that can make good starter homes for families, or enabling homeowners to add ADUs, which can be crucial

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: to creating homeownership opportunities for populations that might not otherwise be able to afford a home or who have different sets of housing needs.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So I am a big supporter of homeownership opportunities, and I certainly didn't mean to cast aspersions on any homeowners by borrowing that term.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: In your view, how much housing would we need to build in the next 10 years to meet demand for New York City?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So the administration recently

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: released a draft report that found in order to accommodate present need to get to a healthier vacancy rate where tenants and others actually have housing options, in order to accommodate projected household growth,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: and then in order to enable people who want to stay in the city to stay in the city,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: that it would be about 700,000 units over 10 years.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And if that was built, we'd meet demand.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: We wouldn't need to build anymore.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, that's the projection.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Obviously, any time you're talking about the future, there are tons of uncertainties.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We don't have control over the macroeconomic condition.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We don't have control over immigration policy, you know, things like that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But my understanding is that that's the administration's best attempt to use information that we have to project 10 years out.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I think the difficulty with trusting those sorts of projections, and you mentioned some of it, the X factors, right, but also the notion that New York City has for its entire history almost been a sought-after place for people to come to,

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: whether it's from other parts of the United States or other parts of the world.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And so there's this sense almost that demand can never be met.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: And there's a lot of discussion in communities now about requiring more and more set-asides of new development to be for people who already call New York home.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: We have very modest set-asides for community district and borough and NYC residents.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: I've been to places around the world where they do subsidies.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: substantially more than us.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: What's your view on mandating more set-asides for folks who have lived here, perhaps even generationally?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thanks for the question, Leader.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't considered that particular question, and I would want to give it more thought.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: That's all I have for now.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Canasio asks Mangin to explain his repeated use of 'fair' and 'fairer' in testimony. Mangin describes his career focus on creating fairer processes ensuring all affected people have a voice in land use decisions, and that everyone should share the burden of creating housing.
chapters.title: CM Canasio Q&A: Mangin on meaning of 'fair' in testimony

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'll pass it on to Council Member Canasio.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Hello, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: David M. Carr
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I also want to thank you for meeting with me a few weeks ago and having a discussion about many of these issues, and I want to thank my colleagues for asking many of the questions that I had already written out for myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I noticed in your testimony, you mentioned the words,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: fair and fairer about five times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And so I'm trying to figure out if you can talk a little bit about what that looks like for you, what that means to you, and why it's so important to highlight it throughout what you mentioned in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, as I mentioned, I think a theme throughout my career has been trying to create fairer processes that ensure that anybody who's affected by a land use decision has a voice in that process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I think that that has not always been the case in New York City.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: As we discussed earlier, I think many of the parts of the city, you know, not least of which, you know,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: your district that experienced some of the pressures of the housing shortage, the high housing costs, the displacement and gentrification pressures,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: that that's a result of not having had sufficient voice in some of the decisions that led to that in the past.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so I think that there are a range of things that we've done in recent years to try to improve on that, whether it's trying to do citywide actions that, again, enable those fantastic conversations about housing, about neighborhoods in the context of the full city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That provide tweaks to land use procedures in order to try to reinforce a somewhat broader perspective over land use decisions that affect a broader population, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So it's part and parcel with, I think, the fair housing focus that I've had over the course of my career, and it reflects itself in process improvements, and it reflects itself in, one would hope, outcomes as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So speaking specifically to everyone should share the burden of creating the housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, that is a much better, pithier way to put it.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Canasio asks how Mangin would treat applications with zero public attendance at community board hearings. Mangin says BSA would rely on the community board's opinion. Canasio then asks about neighborhood character; Mangin explains it's primarily built context and that BSA cannot approve actions affecting neighborhood character, which must go to CPC and Council.
chapters.title: CM Canasio Q&A: Mangin on community board engagement and neighborhood character

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And you talked a lot about community voices and it being paramount.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: We know from the process that the community board is one of those pillars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I am a former community board member for many years, also served as the chair of land use in my community board, a community board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: 11 in Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And I have been witness to many community public hearings on land use items having zero attendees.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Maybe two people might come out and speak at a public hearing at a community board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Do you see that as a

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: approval of a project or lack of engagement of community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: How do you take, how do you see it when you have very little engagement at community board public hearings and how do you plan on

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: using that in your decision-making process?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's a very good question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And back to the conversation I had with the chair around trying to make these institutions like the BSA more open, more transparent, more accessible.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's absolutely true, as you know from your time on a computing board, that many applications don't rise to the notice of a broader public.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But when they do, you want to make sure that institutions like the BSA or like the community board or like the city planning commission

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: are there so that people who aren't frequent flyers can understand what's going on and know how to participate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: But I'm asking if you see that if you're receiving an application and the community board report says no testimony from public, how do you view that as, do you,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What actions would you take in that particular moment to say, is this check off community engagement, local voices were heard?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Is there further conversation needs to happen with the community board?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Like, what does that trigger for you?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, in situations like that, I think that the board would rely on the community board to, you know, their representatives of the community.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: For many applications, you'll have a lot of public voice, people coming to testify, things that can be reflected in the record.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In other situations, as we've all seen, that doesn't happen.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And in that instance, I would hope that the community board would provide their opinion on it so that the BSA could take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In terms of the BSA, so many of the discretionary approvals that the BSA is empowered to grant, which permit developments that are contrary to zoning requirements,

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: require a finding that the proposal will not adversely affect the neighborhood character of an area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: What does neighborhood character mean to you?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yeah, neighborhood character is an absolutely essential finding for the BSA's role within the overall structure of New York City land use.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The neighborhood character finding is there.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Because if an application raises issues of neighborhood character, it could potentially affect neighborhood character, then the BSA can't.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: really touch it.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: They do not have that level of planning discretion.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: If something could affect neighborhood character, then it has to go to the CPC and most likely city council as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, council having the most discretion, CPC having in between more than the BSA but less than council, and BSA being very restricted.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: When it comes to what neighborhood character means, you know, the most obvious is built context of a given neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In certain instances, it can extend beyond that to zoned context, transit access, things like that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So you propose buildings that are out of scale with that immediate context as something that would adversely affect neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, if...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: If the BSA were to approve an application that colorably affects neighborhood character, then that's a significant legal risk.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: They don't have the authority to do that.

chapters.summary: Canasio raises the need for three- and four-bedroom units. Mangin acknowledges the dire need for both small and family-sized units. Canasio then asks about additional transparency measures beyond the website; Mangin cites meeting roadmaps, plain-language descriptions, and community trainings on BSA processes.
chapters.title: CM Canasio Q&A: Mangin on unit size, family housing, and transparency measures

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And we also talked about the vacancy rate having to build a lot more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: I've had many conversations through the land use process where we're constantly

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: weighing out the amount of new units versus the size of those units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: In neighborhoods like mine, we're not just talking about two and three bedrooms, and sometimes we need three and four bedrooms for the families that live in our communities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: So how do you see that as, or what kind of importance do you

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: put weight on when it comes to

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: The actual makeup of the unit versus the amount of units that we're just trying to get online?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think it's incredibly important.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's back to the fair housing focus, back to trying to support housing choice.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That means housing of all types.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: There is a dire need for smaller units.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In New York City, for people who want to live alone but don't have the opportunity, there's also a dire need for family-sized units as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I think we as policymakers in New York City are constantly conscious of, you know,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: the ways that policies can interfere with the full range of housing choices, and in some instances trying to support, say, more family-sized units

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: in affordable housing created through zoning to make sure that at least 50% are two-bedroom or more, things like that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So it's a huge concern, one that we're constantly monitoring and one that I would...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Would stay focused on at BSA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And talk to us about, right?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Awesome.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Love that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: And then in terms of, you know, outside of the amazing website that you're going to build for us that I'm looking forward to, what other transparency measures

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: are you looking to put forth in the BSA to make sure that all of us, community members, everyone's engaged with the process and where things and projects are through the process?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In addition to an accessible website, one that you don't need to be a practitioner to understand, I've also admired ways that the City Planning Commission has become more transparent in recent years.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Even things as simple as like,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: doing a roadmap at the head of a meeting.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Like here are all the agenda items that we're gonna do today so that people who are there to testify or participate understand what's happening and why.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, that's crucial.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I've also mentioned wanting to do trainings for community groups around what the BSA is, what it does, and how to participate.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Now, you can't guarantee that anybody's going to use that and show up.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But when that controversial application comes through, like, I want the infrastructure to be there for those members of the community to participate.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shekar Krishnan
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'd like to now pass it on to Council Member Hanif.

chapters.summary: Hanif asks Mangin to explain BSA's role and discusses his rezoning work including Gowanus. Mangin describes BSA's core function as a safety valve for individual sites facing zoning constraints, detailing variance standards, appeals, special permits, and the BSA Fast Track. He notes neighborhood rezonings require council support and describes working with faith-based organizations.
chapters.title: CM Hanif Q&A: Mangin on BSA role and rezoning experience with communities

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Was that me?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Hi, John.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It's great to see you and hear from you.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And thank you to my colleagues for your questions.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Just want to begin by thanking you for your work over the years, and in particular, your partnership with the New York City Council over several administrations.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Also appreciated you taking the time to visit me in person to discuss your extensive experience in

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: city government and explaining the important role of the Board of Standards and Appeals and what it plays in our city.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I'd like to just state for the record that I think your track record in housing policy, your depth of technical knowledge and experience engaging communities across not just

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: New York City, but several municipalities are all very significant strengths and make you a very strong candidate to serve as chair of the BSA.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I'm really excited about the BSA's authority to fast track publicly funded affordable housing projects, which I know you helped get us.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So first question, for New Yorkers who are not familiar with the Board of Standards and Appeal, could you explain what the BSA does, what the chair's role entails, and how the board's decision can affect communities?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I think there's been a lot of emphasis on homeowners and private property owners.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So, you know, I see the core, core function of BSA as Chair Ong laid out, serving as a safety valve.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, I mentioned the second class I teach every year for Land Use Law.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The first class is the Standard State Zoning Enabling Act from 1924 that lays out the structure of zoning that basically obtains in municipalities across the United States.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: and the BSA is in there.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: They are seen as absolutely necessary when a zoning resolution doesn't allow an individual owner to do anything possible on their site, just because of the interaction with the zoning, with the particularities of the site.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You need a relief valve, somebody you can go to so that you can do something.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That was to save zoning resolutions from significant legal risk.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And to do that, you know, you need to show hardship.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You need to show unique conditions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And BSA only has the authority to grant the minimum amount of flexibility necessary in order for a landowner to build something on their sites.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I feel kind of old school about that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: At different times in history, variant standards have been looser or stricter.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, BSA more recently has returned to its roots on that matter, and I would support that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: They also do appeals when neighborhood residents or when individual landowners don't like determinations of, for instance, DOB, interpretations of a zoning provision.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: BSA is the first stop to try to, if you want to appeal that zoning determination.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Sometimes it goes beyond BSA into the court system, but again, BSA was there to serve as an administrative body that would keep all the different zoning issues that you might face across the city out of the courts.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Otherwise, you might clog the courts with those types of things.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: types of issues.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: BSA administers various special permits in the zoning resolution.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: As part of my work on citywide's MIH and zoning for quality and affordability and City of Yes for housing opportunity, I've helped to create some of those actions as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: For instance, you know,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: parking reductions for certain projects that may have parking requirements that make it difficult for those developments to pencil out.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Or if you're a Wendy's way out in Queens and you need a drive-thru, you have to go through BSA for things like that, or a TD Bank or something like that, you have to go through BSA.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And then, you know, finally, there's the BSA Fast Track.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We've talked a little bit about that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: No projects have gone through that yet.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Would be very excited to stand that up with HPD and other stakeholders in order to create affordable housing projects on sites around the city that just don't have the opportunity under the existing system.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, I mentioned my work with faith-based organizations at City Planning over the last 12 years.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Many of those congregations have land that they want to do things with.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Not all of them have the wherewithal of, you know, a Bishop Hugh Nelson in Brooklyn who went through a major rezoning and then built a bunch of affordable housing or a Christian cultural center that did the same thing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But a BSA fast track for affordable housing will open up opportunities for a significant range of, I think, those faith-based sites that I've talked to over the years as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so I'm excited about that.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: The examples about the hypothetical Buendia's lot and or the drive-through and then

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: adding an ADU, would those decisions be ones that the city council make in the first place?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In general, the types of issues that go to BSA are the teeny tiny ones that are seen not to raise any significant planning or land use issues that should go to CPC or the city council.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And of course, if it's in a local law or if it's in the zoning resolution, council has at some point in the past enacted that provision as well and deemed it not necessary for that action to go to council.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then could you talk a little bit more about the rezonings you've worked on?

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I know you named a bunch, including Gowanus in my district, and how you worked with the council members and affected communities when there were disagreements or competing priorities.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Some of the rezonings that I played the biggest role in, I mean, there was the Soho NoHo rezoning a number of years back.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: There was Inwood rezoning that I participated in.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And then some neighborhood rezonings where I served a more specialized role.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Like I think like in the Jamaica rezoning, I was kind of liaison to many of the faith-based organizations in the neighborhood that wanted to understand what their options were today or under the proposed rezoning.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And, you know, the neighborhood rezonings that I participated in, that continues up till the very end.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Everybody recognizes that council plays a decisive role in those and that without the support of the council, you can't get anything done.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so across administrations, I've seen very earnest efforts to work with city council in order to hammer out those benefits agreements that are necessary in order to get those projects over the top.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Hanif praises the $200 million for NYCHA in Gowanus and discusses challenges with CBA financing. She asks how Mangin's hearings would be more accessible. Mangin commits to transparent websites, community trainings, and emulating practices like plain-language agenda announcements from former DCP Chair Garodnick.
chapters.title: CM Hanif: CBAs, Gowanus investments, and hearing accessibility commitments

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And I agree with...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Some of what you've shared about community benefits agreement.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: I mean, I think for the Gowanus rezoning, you know, 200 million for our two NYCHA developments, and then millions more

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: for climate resiliency projects, and then in a recent rezoning in Windsor Terrace,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: hundreds of affordable housing beyond

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: on MIH.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And, you know, one of the challenges is the financing, where we still keep getting stuck.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And so I certainly have concerns around, you know, these lengthy or detailed community

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: benefits agreements to get projects to the finish line, while also remaining concerned about the cost that is not coming from the city itself.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: It's coming, it has to come from developer or other private means.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So certainly would want to continue.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Seeing how else the city might be able to build affordable housing without needing to dip into these detailed community benefits that

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: are outside of

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: that are in addition to getting the project to move along as opposed to getting a, like trying to pass a strong housing project, but really it's about,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: in my opinion, I think,

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: we need more affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And the community benefits agreements have certainly helped us push projects because they added additional goods in addition to the affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then, you know, the accessibility and openness to the public.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: If confirmed as chair, how would your hearings

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Be different or unique as we've heard you make commitments through this hearing, just your

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: desire to want to engage the council, the broader public, knowing very well that community engagement continues to be, I think, very dire.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Community meetings are not well attended, and specifically the kinds of campaigns that happen to oppose projects and who organizes those remains very concerning.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: So while we've moved a very ambitious City of Yes for Housing opportunity, I would like to see...

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: Of a far greater diversity of New Yorkers participating in not just in-person meetings, but in a multitude of ways.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Right, yeah.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Not every application is going to be, you know,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: is going to have extensive public engagement in it, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But just trying to ensure that the infrastructure is there when projects do come along that have broad interest among the public that they can participate.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In addition to more transparent websites and in addition to

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: you know, community trainings around what the BIA

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: SE is and what it does and how to participate, I think I would emulate some of the previous work under previous city planning chair, Garodnik, who did just very simple things like

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: announce the agenda with like totally understandable descriptions about what was, what each project was about at the beginning of each meeting.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Like just simple things like that go a huge way to making those meetings friendly, friendlier to a broader swath of the public and not just

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: you know, the land use attorneys who have done this 700 times.

utterances.speaker: Shahana K. Hanif
utterances.text: And then finally, and thank you, Chair, what are some of the challenges going into this role or of the BSA itself that you're thinking about?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think that, thank you for the question, I think that

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The biggest outstanding role right now is standing at the BSA Fast Track for Affordable Housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think that that's big.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: My understanding from discussions with existing folks, staff at BSA, is that the board is in a healthy and effective place.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: They do need an IT person, especially if we're going to create these new publicly transparent websites.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But it seems like, if confirmed, I would inherit a pretty well-run ship.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And I'd like to turn it over to Councilwoman Burr.

chapters.summary: Brewer expresses frustration that the Upper West Side is treated as not wanting affordable housing despite having SROs and wanting more affordable units. She asks why every new building can't require affordable housing like some New Jersey cities. Mangin explains the fast track text is in the charter with limited discretion.
chapters.title: CM Brewer Q&A: Mangin on fast track and Manhattan affordable housing

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you for meeting with me.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: As I pointed out, Manhattan is a different world from what everybody else has been talking about.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And the first issue, that fast track, pisses me off, and I'll tell you why.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: To put the West Side, which I have represented for about 20-some years now, in the same bucket with this 12 of other places in the city that do not want affordable housing is absolutely outrageous.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I did a study recently and I listed all the as of right buildings.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: No matter how much I tried, nobody at the city government would say that they would do MIH.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: They would force something.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: They say it's a takings issue, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Even though New Jersey, some of the New Jersey cities are mandating that every new building have affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I'll have two questions.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Why can't we do the same in the city of New York, where every new building has to have some affordable housing, number one?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Number two, would you demand that places like the Upper West Side be taken out of any list?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We have SROs with affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We want more affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We're told constantly, no, we won't put one voucher, one Section 8, one city FEPS, nothing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We only want market to sell.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: subsidize affordable.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I am so tired of that.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So I want to understand in the fast track method, would you take out places like the Upper West Side and give us some more affordable housing?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It sounds like you're referring to the affordable housing fast track, which is a separate

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It is, but you had some say about it when you were at City Planning.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The text that lays out the affordable housing fast track is in the charter at this point, and so there would be extremely limited discretion on how to, there was a rule making.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Did you ever talk about doing it differently, you personally?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: As I mentioned in my responses to council, had expressed concern at one point about trying to ensure

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: that no community districts that were at the highest levels of displacement risk ended up in the fast track.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: When we ran the numbers, it turned out that community districts that are higher on the displacement risk index tend to produce higher amounts of affordable housing so that they were not implicated by the fast track.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay, I'm just saying it is outrageous.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: It is absolutely outrageous.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Number two, at a public meeting at Community Board 8, what was talking about the fact that so much affordable housing

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: units get lost when the obviously east side and west side are becoming more unaffordable.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about rent-stabilized housing being demolished for market-rate development, citing a Gary Barnett building on 96th Street. She then asks about creating a zoning lot map. Mangin says zoning lot determinations require months of historical research and creating a legally effective map remains impossible, citing the 200 Amsterdam case.
chapters.title: CM Brewer Q&A: Mangin on rent-regulated housing and zoning lot mapping

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I think you explained that the only affordable housing you counted was income restrictive housing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Most affordable housing in New York City, but particularly in Manhattan, is rent stabilized or even rent controlled.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Can you talk about the role of rent regulated housing in the city's affordability crisis?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, rent stabilization is absolutely essential to the New York that we know.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's an absolutely essential affordability measure.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's not the only thing that we can or should do to support affordability and affordable housing in New York City, but it's a crown jewel of that system of regulation.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So how would you support rent-regulated housing?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Because in some cases it gets torn down to build rent-restricted.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How would you deal with that?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In the post-urban renewal era, I would say that demolition of large amounts of housing is relatively limited, fortunately.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Well, Gary Barnett just did it on 96th Street and Broadway.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Entire building is empty, was 100% rent stabilized.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's regrettable.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I didn't understand that building.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I would want to look into it more closely.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: In response to a council bill that would require the city to make and maintain a map of

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: zoning lots, you supported the Department of City Planning's position that the making of such a map would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Do you still believe that creating a map of zoning lots is impossible?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The reason I ask, I've done 200 some ULURPs, maybe more, and often the map that is zoning is very strangely

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: designed and the buildings that end up, we have no idea how they get to be merged in such a weird way.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And then we go to court and we lose.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: We want to know about the lots.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, I personally have been involved in months-long processes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: To try to figure out whether a given set of tax lots was in fact a zoning lot or not.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It implicates historical and transactional information that can date back to pre-61, that in some instances can date back

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: even before the zoning resolution.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And given that in many instances, determining whether or not something is a zoning lot takes that much work, that much historical sleuthing, and may end up in court anyway,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, it was and it remains completely impossible to create like a legally effective map.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: of what is and what isn't a zoning lot in New York City, and DOB will certainly tell you the same thing.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But doesn't that make it hard then to fight for housing that is, in our case, too tall, bought too many lots, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: You don't have any sense of that without the lots, right, without the map.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You did have a case in your district.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: 200 Amsterdam Avenue.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Extremely, extremely complicated.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And that, you know, through your advocacy led to changes in how zoning lots are administered in New York City.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But you recognize through that process how intensive it can be.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Time intensive it can be just to figure out the status of one little plot of land.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So to try to do that for the hundreds of thousands, if not millions of lots across the city, it's just not something that's possible.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about HDFCs and BSA's role. Mangin explains HDFCs are the vehicle for publicly sponsored affordable housing and the BSA Fast Track requires HDFC status. Brewer then presses on on-site vs off-site affordable units, arguing off-site in Manhattan sends poor people to lower-income areas. Mangin notes City of Yes shifted to primarily on-site requirements.
chapters.title: CM Brewer Q&A: Mangin on HDFCs and on-site vs off-site affordable housing

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: HDFCs, I think we talked about them a little bit.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: How do you at all figure into what BSA does or will do?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: And HDFCs, if at all.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So HDFCs, or Housing Development Fund companies, those are the state laws.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I was there when they started with Phillips St.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: George.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I know what they are.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So, you know, you and I, when we hear HDFCs,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We may think most immediately of limited equity co-ops in places like the Upper West Side or Lower East Side where I live or North Brooklyn or Northern Manhattan.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: HDFCs are actually a much broader category, however.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: that encompasses basically all newly created affordable housing, whether it's rental or homeownership.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In order to qualify for the BSA Fast Track for Affordable Housing, you have to be an HDFC.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's, again, the vehicle for publicly sponsored affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That requirement in the BSA Fast Track ensures that only projects under public control can go through that process as opposed to a formal rezoning.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Off-site, on-site.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Now, we've had a lot of discussions today about community-based agreements, CBAs.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: The question I have is, when you have a situation with a developer who's building, do you support only on-site in terms of his contribution of affordable housing, or do you support off-site?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: This is a big issue right now in Community Board No.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: My position is very clear, but I want to hear yours.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, I've had a hand in creating various citywide affordable housing programs over the years, starting with MIH.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: MIH does include an off-site option.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It was seen as crucial to provide as many compliance opportunities as we could in the context of a mandatory program to make sure that we were creating affordable housing and enabling housing to be produced.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: While avoiding any kind of legal

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: More recently, we created universal affordability preference as part of City of Yes for Housing Opportunity.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In that, we shifted towards a primarily on-site program.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In order to comply with universal affordability preference, you need to have your affordable units on the same zoning lot.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: With the limited exception of if you had an off-site option before under the old inclusionary housing programs, then you retained an off-site option.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We didn't want to take that away from folks.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But in the main, that shift in housing policy away from a program with an off-site option towards one that's

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: you know, overwhelmingly on site is in line, it sounds like, with your views on the matter.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Okay, I mean, I support on-site because I think otherwise you're supporting basically a racist agenda in the sense that you're sending the poor people elsewhere and letting the rich people be in one location.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That's a Manhattan situation.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Because, so I would like to hear people say on-site only is the way to go.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Just to add, if I may, when off-site options are available, there is a geographic nexus within a half mile or the same community district.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I know, but it's not.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So that you can't ship your affordable units, you know, to some distant land.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: But in Manhattan, that ends up being in a lower income community 100% of the time.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I've seen it 100% of the time.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So even though half a mile sounds like not so far, it actually is a different location.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So you're still supporting.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: off-site if necessary.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned, we've shifted away from, you know, MIH model towards UAP, which is overwhelmingly an on-site.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Would this come up at all at a BSA situation, this type of situation?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I can't imagine offhand a situation where it would, but I can't answer definitively.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Ung asks whether buildings out of scale with context adversely affect neighborhood character, giving a hypothetical 14-story building in R5 zoning. Mangin says BSA cannot approve actions affecting neighborhood character, but notes some R1-R5 areas have tall buildings, making edge cases harder to answer definitively.
chapters.title: Chair Ung round 2: Mangin on neighborhood character and out-of-scale buildings

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And now we're actually gonna move on to the second round of questions.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So I just wanted to start off with a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So back to neighborhood characteristics.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Do you view proposed buildings that outscale the immediate built context as something that you adversely affect the neighborhood character?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So for example, is there any BSA permit or variance that you think would be granted in an R5 or below zoning for a building that would be, let's just say 14 stories with a density equivalent to an R8?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, BSA is not able to approve any actions that would alter the neighborhood character.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So you can say that pretty definitively.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: When it comes to individual applications in individual sites, it's harder to answer that definitively because we do have areas in R1 through R5 that have 30 plus story.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: buildings on occasion.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Or it's very common, for instance, even in one or two family areas, to have pre-1961 six-story buildings around there that could be relevant to neighborhood context.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But, you know, if you're asking about an edge case, like could you put a high-rise in a neighborhood where everything else is two stories, like it seems extremely unlikely that that would be possible.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay, thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Ung asks Mangin to commit that the BSA Fast Track only applies to 100% permanently affordable housing and to specify maximum AMI. Mangin explains the charter uses HDFC state law language, which doesn't require 100% affordable to accommodate limited equity co-ops with non-qualifying residents. He declines to set a maximum AMI, deferring to HPD's soft letter process.
chapters.title: Chair Ung round 2: Mangin on fast track affordability and AMI requirements

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm going to move on to the new BSA zoning permit that's in the Charter Commission proposal.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So given the express intent during the Charter revision process that this new BSA permit

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: was it for the facility 100% affordable housing project.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Will you commit to this council that BSU only grant this new permit to projects when they are in fact 100% permanently affordable income restricted housing?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Very excited about the BSA Fast Track and its ability to facilitate publicly sponsored affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The BSA Fast Track, the charter language, very intentionally picks up the state law language around HDFC.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The state law language around HDFC does not include a restriction for 100% affordable housing, in part, for instance, because over the years,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: HDFCs, limited equity co-ops, or things like that, often include, you know, one or two tenants.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: shareholders, residents who can't meet the income requirements that would therefore kick it out from the BSA Fast Track or HDFC eligibility entirely.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And it's just important in those types of situations to build in a little tiny bit of flexibility so that we're not excluding worthy projects from the pipeline.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But if you look back at the last however many HDFCs that have been used to create homeownership or rental affordable housing, virtually all of them are in fact 100% affordable.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so I don't think that the concerns on that should be too pronounced.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay, so in absence of specified maximum AMI requirements in the charter, how can you assure this body that affordable housing meant to be generated by this new permit will be in fact affordable?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And what would be the maximum AMI you would consider is appropriate for the projects to apply for this permit?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's a great question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So the BSA Fast Track, again, picks up the state law definition around HDFC, which does include income restrictions there as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In general,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think the Charter Revision Commissioners did not want to overly constrain future leadership at HPD over what types of housing projects were

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: and were not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, if you look over the last few administrations in New York City, you go back to Bloomberg era and, you know, affordable housing was being produced at higher AMIs.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Since the de Blasio era through Adams and now in Mamdani, I think the focus has been on much lower incomes.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Would expect that to...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: To maintain into the future, but we wouldn't want to overly constrain future HPDs around the city's affordable housing mandates through charter language, which, after all, require a referendum to change.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So would you today give us a maximum AMI that you would be considered to be appropriate for this project?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's difficult.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: For BSA Fast Track, HPD has to provide a soft letter of commitment for those projects.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so I'm not sure that I would want to go way out of my lane and try to dictate to HPD what they thought was and wasn't an appropriate affordable housing projects in different neighborhoods around the city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In talking to council members, I would say most council members want lower AMI affordable housing, but that is by no means the only thing that council members want.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I've also talked to members who want a full range of mixed incomes, including into middle income, and we wouldn't want to undercut that.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Williams revisits Mangin's article, noting most examples were from New York, not New Jersey as he claimed. Mangin explains he was criticizing overly restrictive open meetings laws that would prevent the council-applicant negotiations that produce CBAs. Williams then asks how his theory that local input defeats affordable housing would be put into practice at BSA; Mangin affirms public participation is incredibly important and community board input remains part of the fast track.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams round 2: Mangin on open meetings law and charter revision theory

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm now going to pass it over to our Deputy Speaker, Williams.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'm back.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I know I said I wasn't going to talk about your writings, but I just have follow-ups from your questions with Council Member Banks.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So I know, and I know when we met you said the same thing around when you wrote those articles, you were referencing some local New Jersey statutes.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Around open meetings law?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: This was one of the...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I was referencing any particular open meetings laws, but just categories of open meetings law that don't exist in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, because as you know, I did read the articles and I was reminded that

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: in that same article, like most of the examples you gave were New York examples.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just wanted to know what were the New Jersey examples, because I know a part of what you said today is like your comments around open meetings law wasn't necessarily in reference to how New York City manages open meetings law and land use decisions.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just wanted to know like,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: What are the Jersey examples?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because in the same article, you only kind of like reference primarily New York.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: New York, D.C., San Francisco.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I would say that the article itself like emerges from my work in New Jersey.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The frame that I was trying to use there was everybody understands exclusionary housing when we're talking about the suburbs, you know,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Haddonfield or Mount Laurel or Cherry Hill or whatever, these areas that have very intentionally zoned to keep out lower income people and people of color.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, a one acre lot minimum, single family home only, you know, there's not a lot of low income folks who are going to be able to live in that jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Everybody understands fair housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: exclusionary housing through a suburban lens.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And it was just an attempt to apply that in an urban lens to neighborhoods and places like San Francisco or DC, where, you know, I spent all my time in DC working in Southeast and Northeast, whereas

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, Northwest was full of leafy green single-family neighborhoods where it was hard to build any multifamily or affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So it was just trying to take a thing that everybody understood and apply it in a somewhat novel context in order to make a point that we should be concerned about building enough housing to ensure we're providing for the needs of the full range of residents of.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Various urban areas around the country.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yes, and in doing that, your opinions about open meetings law, if you just further clarify that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yeah, because I think in your, because I was listening to the exchange with Deputy Leader Banks, and I think in your,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: explanation, you kind of just say like, well, New York doesn't do it like that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so it wasn't really applicable or you didn't see it applicable to New York.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But again, in the same article, you pretty much reference a ton of New York examples.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just want to understand like how you reconcile like what you said and then your opinions about open meetings law, especially considering, you know, BSA does.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Right, right.
