utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: No, that's a great point.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So we're all very familiar with how Euler

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: ULRP works in New York City, and we're all very familiar that for big projects, small projects, projects in between,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: council members are often talking to applicants before ULRP, during ULRP, and then especially at the end of ULRP in order to come to agreements on how to make a project work for a community.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And that might be, you know, modifying the zoning district.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It might be negotiating some additional affordable units like Councilmember Brewer just did around DeWitt Clinton.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It might be negotiating a package of infrastructure improvements like you did around Jamaica.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In some jurisdictions, those conversations would be illegal.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: During the process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You would not be able to talk to a developer at the end of a ULERP in order to try to get what you needed in order to make those projects work for the community.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And the point there is, if you can't have those conversations, what do you think is going to happen?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think a lot of those projects would just get turned down.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Like, if you can't have those conversations to make a project work,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You're just going to say no.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Or maybe they get through with far fewer community benefits than they could in a system like New York where you can have those conversations.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so I was merely criticizing perhaps overly restrictive open meetings laws that prohibit the types of conversations that lead to community benefits agreements.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So one thing that we did.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Mention I just wanted to say is that the charter revision of last year, again, which is still a very sore topic for many in the council,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: especially council members who are a part of those 12 community districts, the residential zonings, which, you know, affect

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: close to like 25 council members.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And for those projects, the council is, well, those members and those community boards are kind of like cut out of the process significantly.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And the Charter Review Commission and their report in defense of that was sort of around some of the conversations we've been having around decisive local input defeats affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so just wanted to know if you can explain why and how this theory would potentially be put into practice.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If you were a BSA chair, I know that the fast track isn't necessarily under the auspices of BSA, but I do think

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Although they are very constrained within BSA, there are some theoretical underpinnings that could potentially be put into practice through BSA.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So just wanted to understand your own opinions about how you would put that particular theory into practice.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: As BSA chair, and just overall,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: your thoughts on what it means to be accountable to the public.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so I agree that, you know, certain communities can be quite difficult when it comes to housing.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I live in one, represent one.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But I do believe that as a lover of a failing democracy, that input does matter and input across.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: The spectrum, not just the people who show up to the community board meetings, but to make sure that there is even diversity within opinions within a community, but that in fact that local input does matter.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, at every stage in my career, I feel like

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Public participation in these processes is incredibly important.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I tend to see, you know, when input is too narrow, when it excludes voices that are affected by those actions, that that can be a problem in terms of fairness, and that type of process can lead to less than ideal outcomes as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So it's incredibly important at BSA or through any process to try to ensure that the full range of voices is heard to these decisions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think improvements have been made around other aspects of the process as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Community board input is part of everything at BSA.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Community board input remains part of the affordable housing fast track that you just mentioned as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And attempts to make community boards more representative of their communities has been another really important aspect.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: aspect of this that we haven't discussed over the last five or ten years.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I think that will also make these processes work better and be more representative of actual community sentiment around some of these projects.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Williams cites NYU Furman Center research showing black homeowners face higher effective property tax rates. She challenges Mangin's written response that housing scarcity drives tax increases. Mangin acknowledges the inequities in the property tax system but argues the housing shortage also hurts homeowners through runaway costs.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams round 2: Mangin on property tax inequity and black homeownership

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: NYU Furman Center found that homeowners in neighborhoods with larger black populations face higher effective property tax rates than homeowners in neighborhoods with larger white populations.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It estimated that homeowners in the quartile of neighborhoods with the largest black population shares would have paid about $17 million less per year if they faced the citywide average effective tax rate.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so you wrote about this in some of your responses to the council.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And so just wanted to know if you agree that property tax inequity is a genuine pressure on black home ownership.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I feel like I'm not familiar enough with that particular research to answer on the fly right now.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You look at NYU, Jonathan.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Why do you not know about the first sentence?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But I completely agree.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm very much aware of the...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Difficulties and and in inequities within the property tax system

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: without being as familiar with them as I could be yeah and the reason why I asked is because in your written response you say that in the city with enough housing homeowner tax increases would be more moderate and so it was just trying to understand how you arrive to that

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: response because I guess

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And I don't think housing scarcity is the only issue.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I think that New York's inequitable property tax system is also a problem that has nothing to do with housing scarcity and the lack of political will, both from previous administrations,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: both state and city are part.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Blame for our property tax system.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

chapters.summary: Williams asks what guardrails Mangin will use to ensure his published views don't predetermine outcomes. Mangin points to his reputation as a conservative interpreter of zoning authority at DCP, committing to follow the text of the law even when it results in less housing, and supporting tightened variance and GCLE requirements.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams round 2: Mangin on guardrails for adjudication vs policy advocacy

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You and I have both heard many times over the years homeowners talk about the fact that, you know, for instance, their kids can't buy a home in the neighborhoods they grew up in.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: They bought their house for X amount back in 1970, whatever, and now prices in the neighborhood are so expensive that they would have never been able to buy, their kids can't buy.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And, you know, what I wrote in my response was just trying to indicate that the housing shortage doesn't just affect low-income renters in particular parts of the city.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It affects us all.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It affects, you know, we hear complaints from lower-density neighborhoods about illegal subdivisions or overflowing trash cans or overcrowded schools.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And some of the runaway housing costs have expressed themselves through, you know, taxes that go up way faster than homeowners who bought in 1970, whatever, are able to keep up with.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And those are all lesser discussed.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: aspects of the housing shortage and that's all I meant to indicate in that response too that the housing shortage hurts homeowners too.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: You have said that you are a by-the-book lawyer and planner and the BSA authority is highly circumscribed.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: If an application comes before you involving a predominantly black homeowner community which

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I have an example of that, and I think I briefly spoke to you about that, where residents submit credible evidence of legally relevant neighborhood impacts.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Can you commit that you will evaluate that evidence on its own merits rather than starting from a presumption that more housing is inherently anti-displacement?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yes, I can commit that I would consider that input on its own merit in terms of, you know, my being a by-the-book lawyer.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Because, you know, to the extent people know me, they know me as like this pro-housing guy, I will often have, you know, questions from lawyers being like, if you interpret the zoning this way, that means, you know, 100 extra units.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Can we get it done?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I can't tell you how often you take a look.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The law doesn't quite support that approach to a particular application or a land use review process, and I will always be the first person to convey that information, despite the fact that it may result in an outcome that results in less housing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Or requires more process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I have no problem with that at all.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: My concern is not whether you and I agree, as you know, we had a very extensive conversation on housing economics.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It's truly whether you can distinguish policy advocacy from adjudication.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So what guardrails will you use as chair to ensure that your published views, although I know very old and people evolve,

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: you know, in reference to exclusionary zoning, supply and neighborhood opposition, do not predetermine how you view the people who appear before you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Right, and thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think the answer to the last question is relevant here, that when facing some of these really difficult zoning interpretation issues at city planning,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: The first stop is always the text of the law that applies in that situation, and it limits what you can do in a given situation, and I have no problem with that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I think, if anything, I'm known at City Planning as being a conservative interpreter of the City Planning Commissions and City Planning's authority, and I would carry that over to BSA as well.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Like I said, being old school around variances, it was not intended to be an end run around rezonings.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It was intended to be a relief valve for sites that meet a very specific set of criteria.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Similarly with...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Some of the GCL waivers for map streets for residential access.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I know

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In recent years, those requirements have been tightened up as well, and I support that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's as it should be.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about BSA's role in NYCHA redevelopment, RAD/PACT conversions, and the Fulton-Chelsea-Elliott project. Mangin says he's unaware of any BSA involvement in that project, though BSA Fast Track could potentially apply to affordable infill on NYCHA campuses. He says large-scale NYCHA redevelopments would go through ULURP, not BSA.
chapters.title: CM Banks round 2: Mangin on BSA's role in NYCHA redevelopment and RAD/PACT

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And now I'd like to pass it off to Deputy Leader Banks.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair, again.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Being the chair of the Public Housing Committee, I want to kind of engage you on NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The BSA's role when it comes to NYCHA redevelopment.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it comes to RAD-PAC conversions or large-scale redevelopment and demolition of NITRA developments, such as Fulton, Chelsea, Elliott, what role?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does the Board of Standards and Appeals currently play?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And did any portion of the Fulton-Elliott-Chelsea redevelopment come before BSA?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And under what circumstances would future NYCHA developments require BSA approval?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Chair.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm unaware of any involvement at all or possible involvement of the BSA in the Fulton-Elliott-Chelsea redevelopment.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: This is speculation, but involvement, BSA, NYCHA in the future,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It is possible for publicly sponsored, affordable infill.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, on a NYCHA campus, it's possible that BSA Fast Track could be an avenue in order to make that happen.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: To do infills?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: To do only affordable.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It would have to be affordable.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So BSA versus ULUP, because there was a ULUP application put in for the redevelopment or the conversion of Chelsea Elliott.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Many residents may not understand the difference between a project that goes to ULUP and one that comes from the BSA.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When NYCHA proposes a major redevelopment involving demolition, new construction, or changes in use, or changes in the physical layout

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: of a campus, what determines whether the proposal must go through ULUP, BSA, or both or neither?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It sounds like the situations you're describing are of such a scale that the BSA would not likely be involved in those types of situations.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, the BSA's legal authority is very constrained.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's cabin to situations that don't involve significant discretion around planning and land use matters.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: For situations that do, you've got to go to CPC and then the council typically.

chapters.summary: Banks asks why the council should trust Mangin to administer provisions he helped create. Mangin says the findings are tightly constrained by law and his involvement is an asset. Banks presses for a concrete example where Mangin would say no to housing; Mangin gives the example of a 10-story building in a two-family district failing the neighborhood character finding.
chapters.title: CM Banks round 2: Mangin on independence as BSA chair despite advocacy background

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, and when it comes to privatization, RADPAC conversions,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: which can result in private entities taking on management and redevelopment responsibilities of public housing developments.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: If a PAC development requires a variance or a special permit or any other action within the BSA's jurisdiction, what responsibility does the BSA

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: have to consider the impact of that action on the existing NITRA residents?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, I'm unaware of any role for BSA in a situation like that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I know in certain instances, NYCHA has been able to pursue overrides that are consistent with public benefit objectives, but I don't think the BSA has a role in the types of applications that you're considering.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Let me go to Independence as the BSA chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You played a major role in the MIH, ZQA, and City of Yes for Housing Opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You helped develop some of the BSA special permits.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You can now basically, well, now, if you all confirm, you'll be overseeing as chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Why should this council be confident that you will administer those provisions independently rather than interpret them in a way that advances?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: the housing policies that you help create?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, like other BSA actions, they are pretty tightly constrained by the findings that were written into those actions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So if an application doesn't meet each and every one of those findings, then the BSA would have no legal authority to approve.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I tend to think my involvement in the creation of some of those BSA actions is a good thing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It will help me if and when any of those applications are before me rather than being something that raises any issues.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, can you...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, I know you spent much of your professional career working to increase housing production, but the BSA chair is not the city's housing advocate.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It's a quasi-judicial position that sometimes requires you saying no.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Give me a concrete example of a circumstance where John may imagine as the BSA chair

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: would be prepared to say, yes, New York City needs more housing, but in a particular project,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: if a particular project should not be approved, but would cause you to reach that conclusion?

chapters.summary: Banks asks what Mangin has learned since writing the 2014 article. Mangin says 12 years at City Planning gave him textured understanding of how land use decisions and politics work. On transparency, Mangin commits to accessible websites, plain-language hearings, community trainings, and guidebooks to help non-practitioners understand BSA.
chapters.title: CM Banks round 2: Mangin on evolution of views and BSA transparency vision

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I fully expect that applicants, potential applicants, will come to the BSA and say, I want to do this.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: the BSA fast track, look at my affordable housing development.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: It's a 10-story building in a two-family district.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: What could be better than all this affordable housing?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And if in the opinion of the board and the staff, it would not be able to meet a neighborhood character finding, then we would inform that applicant before they start the process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so that's an instance where, sure, you might have a planning rationale for that project in that particular location, but if it wouldn't be able to meet the neighborhood character finding, then we will send it on its way.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: We'll send them over to DCP.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Looking back across that record, is there any significant positions you've taken on housing development or community control that you now believe you got wrong?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I would have to think about that and get back to you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Come back.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Nothing springs to mind at this moment.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And can you kind of explain, like, what experience taught you, you know, your experiences that John Madgen, who wrote the Exclusionary Zoning,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: article at that time, what are the things you think you didn't understand that's different now?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Well, I didn't have as extensive on the ground experience

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: with council, with neighborhoods around the city that I did at the time that I wrote that article.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: My first job out of law school, which was prior to writing that article, was with neighborhood groups across the city, and I got to form a number of relationships with many of those groups in all five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But of course, I've learned an immense amount about how land use decision-making processes work, and in particular, you know, the politics behind them, the way

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: that applications can get to yes that I didn't know at that time.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So I agree that the article wasn't about New York, but it didn't have the sort of textured understanding of a lot of these on the ground issues that 12 years at City Planning has helped me to get.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it comes to your vision for the BSA, you said your goal is to make the BSA more open, transparent, and understandable.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What specifically would you change?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it comes to public notice, hearing times, application materials, online records, community outreach, language access, or something else.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How should this council measure whether you succeed or successful?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Again, I would be very keen to make a website that's more accessible to a broader range of potential participants in the process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I would want to make hearings more inviting by more clearly flag posting what's happening.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: At a given meeting and what the different applications are about.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm a lawyer, and so I'm keenly aware of how alienating some of that legal language can be.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so, again, dating back to some of my earliest work in land use and use.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I've got my little guidebooks here where I tried to break down really complicated things like what is ULERP, what is zoning, what is affordable housing at like an eighth grade level.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: So it was really tough sometimes to take the technical legal language governing zoning or ULERP and

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: put it in a way that, you know, folks who don't have that background could understand.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And so it's been a commitment of mine throughout the process, and I would look forward to doing that at BSA as well.

chapters.summary: Banks asks for a commitment that residents opposing projects won't be dismissed as NIMBYs. Mangin commits to carefully listening to all community members, pointing to his first job in land use working with a diverse range of community organizations across the spectrum of housing views.
chapters.title: CM Banks round 2: Mangin on commitment to treat community opponents as stakeholders

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Final, given everything that we've discussed today about your writings and your views on, you know, community participation,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: what commitment can you make that residents who come before the BSA opposing a project will not simply be viewed as being NIMBY or obstacle to housing production,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: but as a stakeholder whose testimony can meaningfully affect the impact of the case that's before you?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: No, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Commit to carefully listening to all members of the community that want to participate in these applications.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And it really does go back to, you know, my first job in land use, where if you look at the community organizations, the neighborhood associations that helped us create these,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: that participated in this process, it's a real range of folks who are rah-rah housing, folks who are way more skeptical of development, folks that are more policy-oriented, folks that are very activist-oriented, and everybody in between.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And the point was just to try to enable all those groups to participate in the process.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And I'm the same person today that, you know, wrote this.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In fact, maybe I should write a guidebook to the BSA and what it does so that more people can understand how to participate.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, that would not be a bad idea.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilor.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The verdict is not out as yet, but thank you.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks about air rights transfers that enable taller buildings, often without affordable housing. Mangin explains BSA typically has no role in workaday zoning lot mergers or landmark TDRs, which go through DCP. BSA only gets involved in controversial zoning lot disputes like the 200 Amsterdam case.
chapters.title: CM Brewer round 2: Mangin on air rights and BSA's role

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Now I could turn it over to Councilmember Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: I just want to know air rights.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: That's what all of my developers buy constantly and then build taller.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: No affordable, usually.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So how would you, if at all, play a role in that issue?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Obviously, in the past, only air rights that we ever know about is as purchased from a public sphere, and now that's been eliminated, so that's not even going to be known to any of us.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So the air rights are, I mean, you'll see a church or a synagogue, and the next thing you know, there's a tall building right next door because they've sold the air rights.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: So how would you play that, if at all, in the BSA role?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Are you referring to, like, the zoning lot mergers that create tall buildings?

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yep, and the air rights.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Yeah, I didn't know if you were referring to those or the landmark TDRs that are...

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: All of the above, I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'll start with landmark TDRs.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm unaware of any process that the BSA would play in landmark TDRs.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: If you need any modifications on a receiving site in order to accommodate landmark TDRs, you have to go to the City Planning Commission.

utterances.speaker: Shaun Abreu
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: In terms of zoning lot mergers, typically the BSA would only get involved when you get, you know,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: more controversial, stickier issues like around the zoning lot for 200 Amsterdam, where BSA was a mere stop on the way to the courts.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: As you know.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But typically for the types of workaday zoning lot mergers that enable development to happen around the city, the BSA would not have a role in those.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Williams asks whether BSA has set criteria for determining neighborhood character, calling it subjective. Mangin explains it's less subjective than it sounds, rooted in case law, with built context as primary and zoning and transit access as secondary factors. Williams raises a specific Jamaica Avenue project that is significantly larger than surrounding R3A/R4 zoning; Mangin says he's unaware of that application.
chapters.title: Deputy Speaker Williams: Mangin on neighborhood character criteria and Jamaica Avenue project

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And I believe the deputy speaker has one more question.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Yes, it's always in your line of questioning with deputy leader banks.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I'm like, oh, I have a follow up.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So neighborhood character, which I think is like a quite subjective power that BSA has.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: I am not familiar, but wanted to know if there are any set criteria to determine neighborhood character.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like, how does that get determined by BSA?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because that, to me, is, like, very subjective.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because you talk to constituents in my district that...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Have their community landmarked and their view of like neighborhood character is very strict versus like other members of my district who have a different opinion that might live, you know, closer to

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: the downtown Jamaica area that has a ton of, you know, new units.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: That's a very good question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Neighborhood character, not as subjective as you might think or as it sounds.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I mean, as you can imagine, there is a lot of case law extending back in time around what it means and what it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know,

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: First and foremost, neighborhoods built context.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Also relevant can be things like zone context, you know, transit access, things like that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But it is not, it's not like up to the board or up to the chair solely to determine that.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: There's a lot of history there.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But is there a set criteria to determine that?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Or like, is it that you use zoning history?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Like, what do you use?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Do you use zoning history?

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Do you use...

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: First and foremost, it would be built context in a neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And then, you know, what's the zoning, what's the neighborhood zoned for as well could be relevant.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Is it right next to a subway stop or is it like three miles away?

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: You know, that type of thing.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: But it's not a completely open field that the board can just make whatever determination they want.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: Because I have a project on Jamaica Avenue that they have told me they're going to go to BSA about.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And in my opinion, outside of the fact that it is transit-oriented development, which fair, we get it, we need to build more near transit hubs.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: But it is significantly larger than the R3A surrounding, R3A, R4 surrounding area.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: So at...

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking because to me it seems, from my perspective, which is why I want to be educated, it seems quite subjective.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: It doesn't seem specific to current neighborhood context because this building is going to produce over 300 units.

utterances.speaker: Nantasha M. Williams
utterances.text: And right around the corner from that is a one-family house.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Gotcha.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: I'm unaware of that particular application.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: And to provide any additional detail on how BSA interprets neighborhood character, I would have to get back to you on that after consulting with them about the program.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Okay, now seeing no other members have questions, Mr.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Manjin, your excuse, and thank you for joining us today and answering all our questions.

utterances.speaker: John Mangin
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Chair, and thank you, Council Members.

chapters.summary: Ung excuses Mangin, opens the floor for public comments, and announces a two-minute limit per speaker with panels of four. Speakers are asked to fill out appearance cards.
chapters.title: Chair Ung opens public testimony and announces panel format

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I am now opening up the floor for public for comments.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: We ask that you please limit your comments to two minutes.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: And if you wish to speak, please fill out an appearance card, the sergeant at arms, and you'll be given an opportunity to make your comments.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Also, if you have a written statement, please provide a copy of that statement to the sergeant at arms.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'll be calling everybody up in a group of four as a panel.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So first is...

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: George James, Tabitha Keneen, Anne Marie Gray, and Frank Clark.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I would just say once one panelist finished speaking, the next one could just start speaking.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: You don't have to wait for me.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So first, I'm going to go with George James.

chapters.summary: Janes, an urban planner testifying as a private citizen, describes his first interaction with Mangin as memorable for being different from typical government dialogue. He calls Mangin temperamentally ill-suited for government service, particularly land use, and plans to submit written testimony with examples of misleading statements during City of Yes.
chapters.title: Public: George Janes opposes Mangin as temperamentally unsuited

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: Hi, I'm George Janes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: I'm an urban planner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: I'm not representing any client here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: I'm here on my own time as a citizen.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: My first interaction with Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: Mangin was about six or seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: And after it, I wrote my DCP contact at the time, quote, you shouldn't let John speak to people, unquote.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: And clearly he's smart.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: Clearly you've heard him speak.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: He's well-spoken.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: And that's not what I meant.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: The interaction was memorable because it was so different from any that I've had with those in government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: While we might disagree, until then, my dialogue with people who serve, especially in planning, has always been one of mutual respect.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: But from that very first interaction, it was clear to me that Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: Mangin operated differently.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: As he showed during the City of Yes, he was there to win, to crush opposition, and to get a job done by any means necessary.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: There are lots of places where this type of hard-charging behavior is appropriate, but

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: Government service is not one of them, especially not in land use.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: In government, the process or how something is done is as important as what is being done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: And that's the issue, and that is why I am here today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: I believe Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: Mangin is temperamentally ill-suited to serving in government at any level, and certainly not in a leadership position.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: I will be submitting written testimony with examples of Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: Mangin's misleading statements and half-truths made on the record during the City of Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: And which will be reflective of my own personal experiences, and I hope you use them as you see fit.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Gray, executive director of Open New York, calls Mangin the most qualified person to run BSA, citing his decade at DCP, his commitment to fair housing, and his dedication to personally hearing every public comment during 13-plus hours of City of Yes testimony. She notes 50% of renters and 45% of homeowners are rent-burdened.
chapters.title: Public: Anne-Marie Gray (Open New York) strongly supports Mangin

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: My name is Anne-Marie Gray.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: I'm the executive director of Open New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: We are a statewide grassroots pro-housing advocacy organization that advocates for more homes and lower rents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Young and members of the committee for allowing me to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: I am in strong support of John Mangin's nomination to chair the Board of Standards and Appeals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: There is no one more qualified to run the BSA than John.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: He spent more than a decade at Department of City Planning, where he worked so closely with council, as we heard, to address the housing crisis through neighborhood planning efforts, as well as crucial initiatives like mandatory inclusionary housing and City of Yes for Housing Opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: I personally worked with John directly in my prior job in city government and have interacted with him as an advocate over the last four years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: And I truly cannot think of anyone more knowledgeable about land use, more committed to fair housing outcomes, or more dedicated to public service.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: I really distinctly remember him sitting in this very room through every single hour of 13 plus hours of testimony, both at the City Planning Commission and City Council hearings for what would become City for All and City of Yes for Housing Opportunity.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: And he did that so that he personally heard every public comment himself.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: And that just is the type of practitioner that he is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: New Yorkers would be so lucky to have him at the helm of this agency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: The fact that John has long acknowledged the basic reality that for decades New York City's approach to housing and land use has led to exclusionary outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: should be a prerequisite for the job, not a disqualification.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: In recent weeks, HPD and DCP released the Fair Housing Growth Strategy, a report in compliance with Local Law 167 that was championed by the City Council at its passage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: And it really confirmed what John has been saying for years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: Far too many New Yorkers have experienced extreme displacement pressures so that the highest income neighborhoods with outsized political power are allowed to essentially close themselves off to new neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: The result is a housing shortage that hurts renters and homeowners alike.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: 50% of renters and 45% of homeowners spend more than 30% of their income on housing alone.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Ms.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Gray, sorry, please wrap it up.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: I really just, I urge you to confirm, John.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: I'm happy to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anne-Marie Gray
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Kanene testifies that Mangin's career making the case for building housing in high-cost neighborhoods is precisely what makes him qualified. She notes the BSA's expanded fast-track authority makes this one of the city's most consequential housing appointments, and his academic writing should be a prerequisite, not disqualification.
chapters.title: Public: Tabitha Kanene (NYC New Liberals) supports Mangin nomination

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: My name is Tabitha Kanene, president of the New York City New Liberals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: I'm here to testify in support of John Mangin's nomination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: Mangin brings a depth of experience that few nominees to this board ever have.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: Early in his career, he worked as a housing litigator.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: And construction manager for Fair Share Housing in New Jersey, an organization born out of the Mount Laurel exclusionary zoning cases, meaning he has seen firsthand what happens when local governments lose the end, use land use law to keep affordable housing out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: He has taught land use and urban planning law for years as an adjunct professor at NYU Wagner.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: And he's a published scholar on zoning policy, having written on the ways land use regulation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: He's up housing costs in high demand cities like ours.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: For the past decade, he has applied that expertise at the Department of City Planning, where he now directs the housing division.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: He led the development of City of Yes for Housing Opportunity, the most significant citywide zoning reform in a generation, along with multiple neighborhood rezoning plans.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: He then served as Director of Policy and Research for the 2025 Charter Revision Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: I understand some members of the body are uncomfortable with this nomination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: I'd ask you to consider why.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: The record shows Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: Manjin has spent his career making the intellectual and practical case

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: for building more housing in high-cost, high-demand neighborhoods, the same neighborhoods that have historically been the hardest to build in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: He helped design the charter revision measures that voters approved by large margins last year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: That history is precisely what makes him the right person for this job.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: The BSA is no longer just a technical body ruling on zoning variances.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: Since last year's charter revision, it has expanded authority to fast-track housing approvals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: That makes this next chair one of the most consequential housing appointments in this city.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: John has the knowledge, experience, and conviction to lead the BSA and use that authority judiciously.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: New York needs more housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: This council should confirm John Manchin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Tabitha Kanene
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Clark, representing 500+ organizations and 250,000 tradespeople, supports Mangin as having the qualifications and judgment BSA demands. He emphasizes Mangin's legal background, land use expertise, and practical understanding of how decisions affect real projects and communities at a moment when the city needs faster housing production.
chapters.title: Public: Frank Clark (NY Building Congress) supports Mangin

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: Good afternoon and thank you Deputy Speaker Williams, Chair Ong, Deputy Leader Banks, Councilmember Brewer and other members of the Council for the opportunity to testify today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: My name is Frank Clark, Chief of Staff of the New York Building Congress.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: New York Building Congress represents over 500 constituent organizations and 250,000 tradespeople dedicated to the growth and prosperity of New York City's built environment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: I'm here today to express our strong support for the nomination of John Mangin to chair the Board of Standards and Appeals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: Mangin brings the qualifications and judgment this role demands at a moment when the city urgently needs the board to help advance housing production.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: As a board whose mandate does not include policymaking or the exercise of broad discretion, the BSA needs a leader who will apply the law carefully, fairly, and without delay.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: That's exactly what Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: Mangeman brings to the table.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: His background as an attorney and his deep experience in land use gives him the tools to handle technical applications with rigor, and his years as a public servant speak to a genuine respect for the institutions he'll be leading.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: His experience navigating both the public and private sectors give him a practical understanding of how land use decisions affect real projects and real communities,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: an understanding that will serve the BSA well as it takes on new responsibilities under the charter revisions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: At a moment when the city is asking its institution to move faster without sacrificing

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: Safety, that kind of grounded, hands-on experience is exactly what's needed.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: Addressing the housing crisis requires increasing housing supply, including affordable housing, and Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: Mangin's experience will help the BSA meet its responsibilities in that effort.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: As the Council exercises its advice and consent role on this nomination, the Building Congress strongly urges you to approve John Mangin's appointment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Frank Clark
utterances.text: Thank you for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - George Janes
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Your excuse.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm going to call the next panel of the next, yes, panel.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Carl Weissbrod, Dan Miller, Jason Cohn, and Brandon Chenney.

chapters.summary: Weisbrod, former DCP chair who hired Mangin in 2014, calls it one of his best decisions. He credits Mangin as the intellectual brainchild behind Mandatory Inclusionary Housing and essential to the East New York rezoning. He describes Mangin as brilliant, collaborative, judicious, and open-minded.
chapters.title: Public: Carl Weisbrod strongly supports Mangin as essential to MIH creation

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: My name is Carl Weisbrad.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: I am a senior advisor at HRNA Advisors, but I'm testifying this afternoon in my individual capacity,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: not as a representative of HRNA, but in strong support of John Mangin's nomination to serve as the chair of the New York City Board of Standards and Appeals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: In 2014, when I was the chair of the City Planning Commission and director of the Department of City Planning, I hired John to come work for the department.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: It was one of the best decisions, but also one of the easiest decisions I made during my tenure at City Planning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: John was and is obviously a brilliant lawyer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: But beyond that, when I interviewed him, it was clear that he was deeply committed to affordability.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: housing and to those many millions of low-income people who have been excluded from safe, habitable, affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: My highest priority initially at City Planning was to fashion a zoning regimen for mandatory inclusionary housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: John Mangin quickly became the intellectual brainchild and a collaborative team leader that enabled MIH to be fashioned and adopted by the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: Indeed, although establishing MIH was certainly a team effort, if one person can be said to have been essential to it, it's John Mangin.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: Today, all of us can be justly proud of the decade-long experience of New York City's deployment of MIH, which has been a model for the nation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: John's positive impact on New York City's affordable housing has gone well beyond mere enactment of MIH.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: The first deployment of the program was the rezoning of East New York in 2016.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: John was essential in fashioning that rezoning, and its success is apparent.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: I will just say John Manchin has the intellectual depth and rigor, but at the same time he is collaborative, judicious, and open-minded.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: At the BSA, all of John's broad and considerable talents will come into play.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: It is hard for me to think of anyone more qualified to take...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Carl Weisbrod
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: On this exciting story.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN
utterances.text: Please.

chapters.summary: Miller, testifying as a private citizen, notes the city needs 70,000 units per year but produces 20,000-30,000. He argues that when the process fails this direly, ordinary New Yorkers pay the price, and urges council to consider impacts on people who aren't local but want to live in New York.
chapters.title: Public: Dan Miller supports Mangin, urging council to consider non-local impacts

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: Hi, my name is Dan Miller.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: I'm testifying just as a private citizen in support of Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: Mangin's nomination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: The council's own required report has found that the city needs to produce about 70,000 units per year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: We're currently averaging somewhere from 20 to 30.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: When the process is failing at this level, when we have a shortage this dire, ordinary New Yorkers like myself are the ones who pay the price.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: And acknowledging that failure

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: does not and should not disqualify a candidate from serving in a position which they're eminently qualified to do so.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: Mr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: Manchin is a brilliant writer and a strong advocate for building more homes, and he's

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: extremely qualified to serve in this role.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: And while local control is important, I want to urge members of the council to also consider the impact of housing decisions on people who aren't local.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: People who, when I moved into my current apartment,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: I didn't just look for homes in one neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: I looked all over.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: over the city, Astoria, Crown Heights, Bushwick, because I wanted to be in New York.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: There are many people across the nation who want to be in New York and can't because we don't build enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: Our current process doesn't let us build enough.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: It's not working.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: John Mangin understands that, and I hope that you won't hold that against him.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Dan Miller
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Cohn argues Mangin brings the expertise, judgment, independence, and commitment to fair government that BSA requires. He says serious engagement with controversial land use questions shouldn't be disqualifying, and disagreement with policy arguments shouldn't be conflated with inability to administer the law fairly. He notes 2 million New Yorkers are rent-burdened.
chapters.title: Public: Jason Cohn (Robin Hood Foundation) supports Mangin

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: My name is Jason Cohn, and I serve as the Chief Public Policy Officer of the Robin Hood Foundation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: For nearly four decades, Robin Hood has worked to elevate New Yorkers out of poverty.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: Housing is central to that mission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: We believe that John Mangin brings precisely the combination of deep expertise, sound judgment, independence, and commitment to fair and effective government that the Chair of the Board of the Standards of Appeals requires.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: Over more than a decade at the Department of City Planning, John has developed an extraordinary command of New York City's zoning and land use framework.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: That expertise is particularly important at the Board of Standards and Appeals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: As chair, the chair must be able to interpret the zoning resolutions, evaluate complicated applications and evidentiary records, and distinguish between broader policy preferences and the legal standards governing the individual matters before the board.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: John's professional experience has prepared him unusually well for those responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: We recognize that recent reports have raised concerns

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: among members of the Council regarding John's academic writing from more than a decade ago in his work on the 2025 Charter Revision Commission.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: His earlier writing should be examined in the context of longstanding questions about exclusionary land use practices, housing production, affordability, and access to high opportunity neighborhoods.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: Reasonable people can disagree with his conclusions or with language used in those debates, but serious engagement with controversial questions of land use policy should not itself be disqualifying for leadership of a land use body.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: Nor should disagreement with a policy argument be conflated with an inability to administer the law fairly.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: The relevant question before the council is whether John possesses expertise, judgment, integrity, independence, and respect for the law necessary to lead the BSA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: We believe he does.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: For Robin Hood, this nomination comes at a moment of an extraordinary urgency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: Two million New Yorkers are rent burdened.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: Our experience reinforces a basic reality.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: New York needs both immediate interventions that keep people in their homes and long-term action that expands the supply and availability of affordable housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: Meeting that challenge requires strong institutions and highly capable servants.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: John meets all those requirements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jason Cohn
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Cheney, representing the NY Housing Conference, testifies in support and submits a letter signed by 47 housing organizations. He calls Mangin highly qualified, noting his attorney training, land use expertise, and experience with public approvals are precisely what BSA needs, and that his testimony today demonstrates his temperament and patience.
chapters.title: Public: Brendan Cheney (NY Housing Conference) supports Mangin with 47-organization letter

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: My name is Brendan Cheney.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: I'm Director of Policy and Operations at the New York Housing Conference.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: New York Housing Conference is a nonprofit affordable housing policy and advocacy organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: As a broad-based coalition, our mission is to advance city, state, and federal policies and funding to support the development and preservation of decent and affordable housing for all New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: We are testifying today in support of the nomination of John Mangin as the chair of the Board of Standards and Appeals.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: He is highly qualified for the position, and we're excited for him to bring his expertise and experience to the role to help address the housing crisis.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: I'll summarize a little bit just in the interest of time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: John Mangin's training as an attorney, expertise in land use and planning, and experience with the administration of applications for public approvals are precisely the type of background needed for the leader of the BSA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: As a career public servant who recognizes the severe affordability implications of our housing supply crisis, his appointment is particularly suited to the current crisis and his work has consistently displayed a commitment to the integrity and value.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Of the role of government.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: And I think just in seeing his testimony today, I think you can see that he has the temperament and the patience for the role as well.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: So therefore, as the council performs its advice and consent on John Mangin's nomination, we strongly urge it to approve his appointment.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: You'll also see that included with our testimony is a letter that we've included that's got...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: signatures from 47 other housing organizations also supporting John Mangin's nomination.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Brendan Cheney
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'm happy to answer any questions.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Thank you all for your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: You're all excused.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm going to call up the next set of panelists, and with that, I'm going to go on to the Zoom panelists.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: First, we have former council member Dan Garanek, Jeffrey Thomas, Mulan Mehta, and Luke Levenway.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Apologies.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm going to go to Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: You'll come back to in-person.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: So it's just one panel on Zoom, and then we'll come back in person.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: I'm going to ask the panelists on Zoom to unmute themselves.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Yes, please go first.

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: You may begin.

chapters.summary: Thomas, a central Brooklyn resident, shares a story about a development project near his church that was delayed when the developer sold the site after council modifications. He argues Mangin is an excellent choice for the technical economic role of BSA chair, and that policy should continue coming from the council.
chapters.title: Public (Zoom): Jeffrey Thomas supports Mangin for technical economic role

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: Are you speaking to me?

utterances.speaker: Sandra Ung
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please go for it.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: Don't mean to go ahead of such a distinguished speaker, but my name is Jeffrey Thomas.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: I'm a resident of central Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: Thank you all for the opportunity to be here again virtually.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: I was at City Council about a year and a half ago as you all were discussing a project that's two blocks down from my church.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: I supported that project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: It was going to bring affordable housing as well as market area housing to an area that badly needed more supply.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: And I remember telling the council at that time, I don't support it because I care about the profits of the developer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: I just want to make sure it gets built.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: If they only make a couple of cents of profit, I don't care as long as it gets built, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: And we had other community members testifying, some saying the developers could certainly build many more affordable units while still making it able to successfully build the project.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: The council approved the reasoning with modifications, which I thank you all for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: And then we found out about a month ago that the developers finally decided that isn't going to work for them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: They sold the site to another developer that thinks, okay, they can make it work, but they can only make it work at the cost of more studios, more one bedrooms, fewer family sized homes, more market rate, one person housing.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Jeffrey Thomas
utterances.text: And
